column1: At the outset

column9: it held

column11: whose purpose is to protect the “sphere of intellect and spirit” from “official control.” As Justice Robert Jackson wrote for the Court

column17: religion

column1: The Constitution Does Not Allow Overbreadth
Laws are said to be overbroad if
column2: in addition to whatever else they might appropriately prohibit
column3: they significantly restrict protected First Amendment freedoms. Overbreadth takes what might be a legitimate use of law or regulation and extends it into areas where it threatens freedom itself. Often
column4: when a provision of a law violates the First Amendment
column5: it is possible to salvage the rest of the law by cutting out the offending section. For example
column6: a law prohibiting both physically assaulting and criticizing an official could be successfully challenged
column7: but that challenge would lead to the removal of the ban on criticism and not bring down the ban on physical assault. However
column8: laws may be stricken in their entirety as overbroad if it is impossible to separate their constitutional and unconstitutional provisions without writing a completely new law.

It was on grounds of overbreadth that a graduate student at the University of Michigan successfully challenged the University of Michigan’s speech code in Doe v. University of Michigan (1989). The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan found that the code was blatantly overbroad in prohibiting

column5: speech that “victimizes an individual on the basis of race … and that … creates an intimidating
column6: hostile or demeaning environment for educational pursuits.” Similarly
column7: in DeJohn v. Temple University (2008)

column9: noting that the policy—which prohibited

column11: “generalized sexist remarks and behavior”—“provide[d] no shelter for core protected speech
column12: ” and thus violated the First Amendment rights of all Temple students. Many attempts to regulate speech share this very common but fatal flaw of overbreadth
column13: because it is difficult to craft laws restricting expression that do not prohibit some constitutionally protected speech. It is a very good thing

column1: How and Why the Constitution Does Not Permit Vagueness
The Constitution requires that our laws be written with enough clarity so that individuals have fair warning about what is prohibited and what is permitted conduct
column2: and that police and the courts have clear standards for enforcing the law without arbitrariness. (One can imagine how easy it would be for police officers to arrest only those whom they dislike if the laws could be molded into any interpretation.) In Grayned v. City of Rockford (1972)
column3: the Supreme Court held that a statute or regulation is unconstitutionally vague when it does not “give a person of ordinary intelligence a reasonable opportunity to know what is prohibited
column4: so that he may act accordingly.” Without a prohibition against vague rules
column5: life would be a nightmare of uncertainty regarding what one could or could not do. When faced with vague laws
column6: the average citizen would refrain from many lawful
column7: constitutionally protected
column8: and profoundly important activities in order to avoid crossing a vague line that is hard to discern. The courts do not demand mathematical certainty in the formulation of rules
column9: but they can declare a law “void for vagueness” if people of common intelligence would have to guess at its meaning or would easily disagree about its application.

column1: The strictness of the requirement of clarity in any particular case depends on the extent to which constitutional rights and values are involved. Codes that do not directly involve matters of special constitutional concern can be written loosely. For example
column2: ordinary disciplinary rules regulating antisocial conduct at colleges and universities are not held to a very high standard of precision and specificity. (The issue of vagueness as applied to ordinary disciplinary rules is taken up in detail in FIRE’s Guide to Due Process and Fair Procedure on Campus. ) By contrast
column3: rules that touch on First Amendment freedoms must be written with exacting clarity: If individuals are afraid to speak their minds because of the possibility that their speech would be found illegal
column4: they will likely refrain from speaking at all
column5: or at least refrain from saying anything controversial (or perhaps even anything important). A rule prohibiting “bad speech
column6: ” for example
column7: would leave everyone afraid to speak. Speech
column8: therefore
column9: would be

column11: “chilled”—that is
column12: inhibited
column13: diminished
column14: or stifled. Preventing this “chilling effect
column15: ” so that free people may speak their minds without fear
column16: is one of the essential goals of the First Amendment.

column8: the problem with such savings clauses is that while they save laws from being overbroad

column10: but then says that everything protected by the Constitution is not prohibited? The very purpose and effect of such laws are to create a chilling effect by confusing individuals who would speak on any subject that might draw a complaint
column11: or by sending the message that a student speaks at his or her own peril. Imagine a law forbidding “annoying” religious practice and worship that added a savings clause with an exemption for the free exercise of religion protected by the Constitution. Savings clauses do not make unconstitutional laws constitutional—they only shift the defect from overbreadth to vagueness.

column1: In his opinion enjoining the enforcement of San Francisco State University’s civility policy in College Republicans at San Francisco State University v. Reed
column3: U.S. Magistrate Judge Wayne Brazil eloquently illustrated the constitutional flaws of savings clauses
column4: writing:

column1: We must assess regulatory language in the real world context in which the persons being regulated will encounter that language. The persons being regulated here are college students
column2: not scholars of First Amendment law. What does a college student see when he or she encounters section 41301? That student sees a long list of mandates and proscriptions
column3: most of which seem to describe
column4: in terms relatively familiar to the student and with a fair amount of particularity
column5: various forms of “Unacceptable Student Behaviors.” After seeing all these prohibitions

column3: after the fact
column4: that the course of action she chose was protected by the First Amendment? To us

column1: How and Why the Constitution Does Not Allow Viewpoint Discrimination

It should go without saying that public colleges and universities (or private colleges and universities that promise constitutional levels of academic freedom and liberty of expression) may not regulate speech on the basis of the point of view it conveys. Viewpoint discrimination is
column2: as Justice William Brennan put it
column3: “censorship in its purest form.” As discussed earlier
column4: the history of censorship is full of examples of viewpoint discrimination (as in the Alien and Sedition Acts
column5: which did not ban any and all speech about the president or about politics
column6: but only speech that was critical of the president). Laws that ban only certain viewpoints are not only clearly unconstitutional
column7: but are also completely incompatible with the needs
column8: spirit
column9: and nature of a democracy founded upon individual rights.

column1: Most censors practice viewpoint discrimination
column2: wishing to censor only speech with which they disagree or that they find offensive. Viewpoint discrimination is prohibited
column3: however
column4: not only by the First Amendment
column5: but also by the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of “equal protection of the laws
column6: ” which requires that the government apply the same rules equally to people in similar circumstances.

column1: In Rosenberger v. University of Virginia (1995)
column2: the Supreme Court overturned a University of Virginia rule barring student group recognition for any association that “primarily promotes or manifests a particular belief in or about a deity or an ultimate reality.” The Court held that the rule was unconstitutional because while it allowed antireligious perspectives on theological questions and cultural issues
column3: it prohibited religious perspectives on those same issues.

column1: Viewpoint discrimination is distinct from content discrimination . Content discrimination relates primarily to the general subject matter of the speech in question. For example
column2: a decision by a college to open a campus “speaker’s corner” to “discussions and debates on the subject of economics” discriminates on the basis of content (no speech except speech about a particular subject matter
column3: economics) but not on viewpoint. Viewpoint discrimination would occur if the college opened the corner to discussions and debates on economics but prohibited any discussion
column4: for example
column5: that was hostile to free markets.

column1: Content discrimination is sometimes permissible
column2: depending on the location of the speech and the breadth of the speech regulation. Viewpoint discrimination is virtually never permissible. Later
column3: this Guide will address what are known as “time
column4: place
column5: and manner” restrictions on speech. It is in that area of law that the distinction between content discrimination and viewpoint discrimination becomes critically important.

column1: The Use of Student Activity Fees
Public colleges and universities may collect mandatory fees from their students to support extracurricular activities on campus. As the Supreme Court ruled in University of Wisconsin v. Southworth
column3: requiring students to pay such fees is constitutional as long as the university forbids its officials or agents from considering a group’s viewpoint when deciding whether to fund it. As the Supreme Court held in Rosenberger (see above)
column4: denying funding to a group because of the viewpoint it advocates violates the First Amendment’s prohibition on viewpoint discrimination. The subject of student activity fees is taken up in detail in FIRE’s Guide to Student Fees
column5: Funding
column6: and Legal Equality on Campus . At a private campus that advertises itself as open and as not discriminating on grounds of religion
column7: of course
column8: such viewpoint discrimination in the use of student activity fees would be immoral and well might be a breach of contract.

column1: How and Why the Constitution Does Not Allow Prior Restraint

Prior restraint” refers to the practice of prohibiting publications or speech before they are published or communicated (think of restraining individuals prior to their speaking). This is distinct from the more common type of censorship: punishing speech after it has been uttered. Prior restraint is one of the most ancient
column2: primitive
column3: and effective forms of censorship. The traditional example of a “prior restraint” is the print licensing system the Crown of England relied upon in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries
column4: against which John Milton
column5: quoted in our Preface
column6: wrote so eloquently. Under the licensing system
column7: books were reviewed for content before they could be printed. If the Crown disagreed with the content or tone
column8: it could prevent the book from going into print. Even before the United States became a country
column9: English legal minds recognized that prior restraint was the enemy of a free people. American courts have continued this proper fear of and hostility to such a remarkable power of censorship
column10: repeatedly holding that prior restraint on speech and publication is almost never permissible. In typical censorship
column11: an individual utters the prohibited words
column12: his or her fellow citizens hear or read them
column13: and the individual then faces governmental action for such speech. However
column14: where there is prior restraint
column15: the general public never learns what it is that the government does not want a fellow citizen to say and the public to hear. Prior restraint is a profoundly serious threat to liberty.

column1: Unconstitutional prior restraint can take many forms
column2: such as requiring that students get prior approval of the content or viewpoint of campus demonstrations; denying the use of a public theater for showing a controversial production; imposing broad restrictions on public speaking and reporting; banning leafleting; or enacting a rule that allows local officials unfettered discretion to decide who is allowed to organize a parade. The most typical instance where prior restraint occurs is when a state body
column3: such as a public college or university
column4: requires that speech of any kind must receive prior approval.

column1: The legal presumptions against prior restraint are extremely strong. For example
column2: in New York Times v. United States (1971) the Supreme Court ruled against suppressing the publication of the “Pentagon Papers
column3: ” classified Department of Defense documents relating to the United States’ involvement in Vietnam
column4: despite the fact that some justices recognized that their release might even harm national security . In order to qualify for a prior restraint court order
column5: material about to be published must have a clear
column6: immediate
column7: and devastating impact on national security. The classic example of permitted prior restraint would be a ban before publication of the schedule or route of troop ships in time of war (such publication likely would be ordered postponed until the ships have arrived). Because the presumptions against prior restraint are so powerful
column8: public university students should feel quite confident that their university is breaking the law if it tries to limit their speech through the use of a prior restraint.

column1: Some narrow exceptions exist that allow the government to screen films before they are released—for example
column2: to decide if they are obscene. However
column3: even these procedures need to be swift
column4: governed by explicitly stated standards
column5: and viewpoint neutral. In the rare cases where some campus prescreening is allowed (placing a flier on a campus bulletin board reserved only for events approved by the student government
column6: for example) the criteria must likewise be explicit
column7: standardized
column8: and unrelated to the viewpoint expressed.

column1: The Student Press and Prior Restraint

Some public universities have policies that require all student newspapers to be submitted to an advisor before they are published. Federal (and state) court decisions strongly suggest that this practice is unconstitutional. Furthermore
column2: if these policies give any member of the administration of a public university the right to edit content on the basis of viewpoint—either explicitly or in practice—then such policies will almost certainly be struck down in a court of law.

column1: Censors may attempt to justify prepublication review by citing a case discussed previously in this Guide
column2: Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier (1988). As you will recall
column3: Hazelwood limited the rights of high school journalism students who printed a school newspaper as part of a journalism class. The Court ruled that
column4: under those circumstances
column5: the school could regulate so-called “school-sponsored” speech (the administration acting
column6: in effect
column7: as the publisher) as long as the regulation was related to “reasonable pedagogical concerns.” Thus
column8: the school skirts the prior restraint doctrine through the fiction that the high school itself is the editor of the school newspaper and therefore enjoys editorial control.

column1: Unfortunately
column2: one court has applied Hazelwood to a university newspaper. In the 2005 case of Hosty v. Carter
column3: the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit found that Patricia Carter
column4: Dean of Student Affairs and Services at Governors State University
column5: had not violated the First Amendment rights of student editors of the student newspaper by requiring that the paper must be reviewed by school administrators prior to publication. The court’s analysis made clear that it believed that Hazelwood was equally as applicable to college campuses as it was to high schools. Despite the clear conflict with cases decided before Hazelwood that already had made it quite clear that that prepublication review is impermissible
column6: the Supreme Court declined to review the Seventh Circuit’s decision.

column1: Thankfully
column2: the effect of Seventh Circuit’s almost certainly erroneous
column3: anomalous ruling in Hosty has been limited. Indeed
column4: in response to Hosty
column5: several states have passed legislation protecting collegiate student journalists and expressly forbidding administrative prior review of the type at issue in Hosty . For example
column6: Illinois’ College Campus Press Act was passed in 2007 and effectively renders the Seventh Circuit’s decision moot on all public campuses in the state.

column1: FIRE’s position is that colleges and universities should never seek editorial control over student newspapers and that the application of Hazelwood to colleges is both legally incorrect and morally wrong. Even at private universities
column2: if a school’s newspaper is run by students
column3: university officials should neither want nor use the power to review each issue before it goes to print. Student media plays an important role in educating and bringing issues to the campus community. Universities that do not allow a free student press deprive the campus community of an important component of the open discussion
column4: debate
column5: and expression that universities exist to foster.

column1: Harassment Codes on Campus
Federal law requires that colleges and universities prohibit discriminatory harassment—that is
column2: harassment directed at an individual because of his or her status as a member of a protected class—on their campuses. Specifically
column3: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 prohibits sexual harassment; Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits harassment on the basis of race
column4: color
column5: or national origin; Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 prohibits harassment on the basis of disability; and the Age Discrimination Act of 1975 prohibits harassment on the basis of age. Speech constituting harassment in violation of these statutes is not protected by the First Amendment.

column1: To understand whether your school has a true (and legal) discriminatory harassment code or a speech code disguised as such
column2: you first need to understand what type of behavior the law defines as genuine discriminatory harassment.

column1: Defining Harassment on Campus
In the landmark case of Davis v. Monroe County Board of Education (1999)
column2: the Supreme Court defined student-on-student hostile environment harassment as conduct “so severe
column3: pervasive
column4: and objectively offensive that it effectively bars the victim’s access to an educational opportunity or benefit.” By definition
column5: this includes only extreme and usually repetitive behavior—behavior so serious that it would prevent a reasonable student from receiving his or her education. For example
column6: in Davis
column7: the conduct found by the Court to be actionable harassment was a months-long pattern of conduct including repeated attempts to touch the victim’s breasts and genitals and repeated sexually explicit comments directed at and about the victim.

column1: Harassment
column2: properly understood and as defined by the Supreme Court
column3: refers to conduct that is (1) unwelcome; (2) discriminatory (3) on the basis of a protected status
column4: like gender
column5: race
column6: disability
column7: or age; (4) directed at an individual; and (5) “so severe
column8: pervasive
column9: and objectively offensive
column10: and … [that] so undermines and detracts from the victims’ educational experience
column11: that the victim-students are effectively denied equal access to an institution’s resources and opportunities.”

column1: It is worth reviewing each element of this definition. First
column2: for conduct to constitute sexual harassment
column3: the behavior in question must be “unwelcome
column4: ” which means that the victim or victims found it “undesirable or offensive
column5: ” and did not welcome
column6: invite
column7: seek out
column8: or encourage it. Next
column9: the behavior needs to be not only discriminatory
column10: but also discriminatory on the basis of the victim’s protected class status—in other words
column11: it needs to be negative behavior prompted by the victim’s race
column12: gender
column13: age
column14: or disability. The behavior also needs to be aimed at an individual
column15: rather than just general
column16: broad-based actions without a specific target
column17: and must be sufficiently severe and pervasive to drive a person off campus
column18: depriving that person of his or her right to receive an education. “Objectively offensive” is an important requirement
column19: because it shifts the consideration of the behavior from the subjective experience of a particular person (who might be very easily offended) to the experience of reasonable men and women. This is vital
column20: making the standard for what is legally intolerable not the sensibilities of this or that possibly hypersensitive person
column21: but rather the sensibilities of a typical
column22: reasonable person. The behavior has to be both objectively offensive and perceived by the victim as offensive. Finally
column23: the requirement that the behavior effectively deny “equal access” is also crucial
column24: because it limits discriminatory harassment to conduct that is not only severe or pervasive and objectively offensive
column25: but also so outrageous that it has the “systematic effect” of preventing the victim from getting an education.

column1: Put simply
column2: to be legally punishable as harassment
column3: students must be far more than simply rude or offensive. Rather
column4: they must be actively engaged in a specific type of discrimination
column5: as defined by law. Under this doctrine
column6: there is a pattern of behavior that may involve speech so strikingly awful and persistent
column7: and so focused on a person’s status as a member of a protected class
column8: that the law must treat it not simply as speech
column9: but as discriminatory behavior that constitutes a civil rights violation. Precisely because the Supreme Court cases describe only very extreme forms of speech as “harassment
column10: ” we believe that it makes good sense to think of speech-as-harassment in terms of time
column11: place
column12: and manner restrictions that the Constitution permits: If the speech is repeated
column13: is uttered at inappropriate times and places
column14: and is so uncivilized and pervasive so as to make the victim unable to attend to his or her studies and other activities
column15: then it risks being prohibited and punished. In other words
column16: protected speech cannot become unprotected harassment merely because of its message; rather
column17: to qualify as harassment
column18: one must consider how
column19: when
column20: and where the message was communicated.

column1: Why the Davis Standard is Right for Campuses
Davis v. Monroe County Board of Education (1999) dealt with the harassment of a grade school student
column2: not a college student. Further
column3: the case did not concern a First Amendment challenge to a harassment code
column4: but rather involved a student’s suit for damages against her school following its failure to adequately respond to allegations of harassment. As such
column5: it may seem like a curious source for a definition of hostile environment harassment in the college context.

column1: But because the Supreme Court has yet to decide any case that answers precisely the question of how far a university may go in prohibiting unpleasant speech in the name of preventing discriminatory harassment
column2: the Court’s decision in Davis remains the Court’s only consideration of student-on-student discriminatory harassment. As such
column3: it is the only authority courts
column4: colleges
column5: attorneys
column6: and students have when considering what campus behavior may properly be deemed harassment—and thus unprotected by the First Amendment. For this reason alone
column7: it would be useful
column8: but there are further strong arguments in favor of using the Court’s Davis standard.

column1: For one
column2: the standard announced in Davis carefully respects First Amendment rights
column3: addressing only that behavior that deprives another student of the ability to obtain an education. Davis provides an exacting
column4: speech-protective definition of harassment
column5: ensuring an appropriate balance between freedom of expression on campus and the importance of establishing an educational environment free from harassment. And while Davis took place in the context of a grade school
column6: it provides at least a floor for determining what speech a college may restrict in the name of combating harassment
column7: given that college students enjoy far more robust speech rights than grade school students do.

column1: Moreover
column2: because of the precision of the standard
column3: it has been relied upon by courts
column4: colleges
column5: and legal counsel across the country for more than a decade. As discussed below
column6: courts have time and time again overturned unconstitutional harassment codes on free speech grounds. Because of the specificity and precision of the Davis standard
column7: and its attentiveness to free speech concerns
column8: it is not likely to ever be overturned. As a result
column9: use of the Davis standard increases clarity and certainty on campuses across the country. Students should argue that reliance on Davis is a failsafe way of ensuring that a university will not find itself on the losing end of a free speech lawsuit. Indeed
column10: the Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights (OCR)
column11: the federal agency tasked with enforcing Titles VI and IX on campuses
column12: has also relied on Davis . In its guidance letters
column13: OCR has repeatedly noted that its understanding of hostile environment harassment is informed by and consistent with the Court’s decision in Davis . Given these explicit and repeated invocations of Davis as guiding precedent when it comes to the intersection of free speech and harassment on campus
column14: the Davis standard is now properly understood as persuasive legal authority in determining what conduct constitutes actionable harassment on a college campus.

column1: The Misuse of Harassment Codes
As discussed above
column2: universities are legally obligated to maintain policies and practices aimed at preventing genuine harassment from happening on their campuses. Today
column3: virtually every campus has a code that prohibits students from engaging in discriminatory harassment. In general
column4: there are two types of such codes. First
column5: there are codes prohibiting true discriminatory harassment—that is
column6: behavior that meets the Davis standard . This is the precise kind of discriminatory harassment that federal law says universities must prohibit. Under the anti-discrimination laws listed above and Department of Education rules
column7: any educational institution—from a primary school to a research university—that actively ignores such discriminatory harassment on campus may lose its federal funding. Even more importantly
column8: schools are liable for monetary damages in lawsuits by students harmed by the school’s failure to prohibit real discriminatory harassment. Schools that do not have procedures for preventing harassment find themselves at legal and financial risk.

column1: Second
column2: however
column3: there are codes that claim to ban discriminatory harassment but that
column4: in fact
column5: ban constitutionally protected expression. In other words
column6: under the guise of their obligations under federal law to prohibit discriminatory harassment
column7: universities frequently prohibit speech that does not rise to the level (or even close to the level) of seriousness necessary to constitute unprotected harassment. Universities commonly call these disguised speech codes “discriminatory harassment codes” or “harassment policies” to convince people that they do not pose First Amendment problems and are in fact required by law.

column1: The misapplication of harassment regulations became so widespread that in 2003
column2: the federal Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights (OCR)—responsible for the enforcement of federal harassment regulations in schools—issued a letter of clarification to all of America’s colleges and universities. The letter was very clear about the limits of discriminatory harassment regulation:

column1: Some colleges and universities have interpreted OCR’s prohibition of “harassment” as encompassing all offensive speech regarding sex
column2: disability
column3: race or other classifications. Harassment
column4: however
column5: to be prohibited by the statutes within OCR’s jurisdiction
column6: must include something beyond the mere expression of views
column7: words
column8: symbols or thoughts that some person finds offensive.

column1: The letter further emphasized that “OCR’s regulations are not intended to restrict the exercise of any expressive activities protected under the U.S. Constitution
column2: ” and concluded that “[t]here is no conflict between the civil rights laws that this Office enforces and the civil liberties guaranteed by the First Amendment.” This letter forecloses any argument that federal anti-harassment law requires colleges to adopt policies that violate the First Amendment.

column1: Unfortunately
column2: OCR’s letter has thus far failed to stem the misuse of harassment codes. Indeed
column3: FIRE’s annual survey of speech codes continues to reveal that many so-called harassment codes are in fact speech codes in disguise. (Every year
column4: FIRE examines hundreds of campus harassment codes and compiles them on its website at www.thefire.org/spotlight.) As of this writing
column5: only a minority of harassment codes limit themselves to prohibiting discriminatory harassment in compliance with federal laws. Most universities do not directly follow the Davis standard—that is
column6: requiring the conduct in question to be “so severe
column7: pervasive
column8: and objectively offensive that it effectively bars the victim’s access to an educational opportunity or benefit”—but either ignore it altogether
column9: or modify it in various ways. These modifications tend to contort the regulations and to make the codes unconstitutionally overbroad
column10: prohibiting too much protected speech. Harassment codes often prohibit “verbal conduct” or “verbal behavior” that is demeaning
column11: upsetting
column12: or offensive to members of protected groups. In a free society
column13: however
column14: speech is permitted to demean
column15: upset
column16: and offend (indeed
column17: much honest criticism and polemic aims to do precisely that)
column18: and such speech is protected by the First Amendment. Protected speech certainly does not qualify as discriminatory harassment.

column1: These disguised speech codes have been consistently rejected by the courts. The first of these decisions is Doe v. University of Michigan (1989)
column2: discussed earlier
column3: in which the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan struck down the University of Michigan’s “discrimination and discriminatory harassment” code on grounds of overbreadth and vagueness. The code had prohibited any speech “that stigmatizes or victimizes an individual” on the basis of protected group membership (e.g.
column4: race or sex) that has the “effect of interfering with an individual’s academic efforts.” As should by now be quite clear
column5: such a rule fails to accurately describe the concept of discriminatory harassment. Rather
column6: the code prohibits essentially any offensive speech
column7: without reference to its being so severe
column8: pervasive
column9: and objectively offensive that it has the systemic effect of denying equal access to education.

column2: in an exceptional string of victories for free speech on campus
column3: federal and state courts across the country have consistently struck down unconstitutional speech codes masquerading as legitimate speech regulations at public universities over the past twenty years. In addition to Doe
column4: similar results were reached in UWM Post v. Board of Regents of the University of Wisconsin (1991)
column5: a discriminatory harassment policy; Dambrot v. Central Michigan University (1995)
column6: a discriminatory harassment policy; Corry v. Stanford University (1995)
column7: a harassment by personal vilification policy; Booher v. Board of Regents of Northern Kentucky University (1998)
column8: a sexual harassment policy; Bair v. Shippensburg University (2003)
column9: a racism and cultural diversity policy; Roberts v. Haragan (2004)
column10: a sexual harassment policy and free speech zone; College Republicans at San Francisco State University v. Reed (2007)
column11: a civility policy; DeJohn v. Temple University (2008)
column12: a sexual harassment policy; Smith v. Tarrant County College District (2010)
column13: a “cosponsorship” policy and free speech zone; and McCauley v. University of the Virgin Islands (2010)

column1: Both UWM Post and Booher recognize the core principle that the First Amendment’s fundamental guarantee of free speech trumps any requirements imposed by federal statutes or regulations. As the court put it in UWM Post : “Since Title VII is only a statute
column2: it cannot supersede the requirements of the First Amendment.” As we have seen
column3: the Office for Civil Rights of the Department of Education has stated the same obvious constitutional truth: “Harassment
column4: however
column5: to be prohibited by the statutes within OCR’s jurisdiction
column6: must include something beyond the mere expression of views
column7: words
column8: symbols or thoughts that some person finds offensive.” Remember
column9: Davis prohibits speech that is (1) unwelcome
column10: (2) discriminatory
column11: (3) directed at an individual (4) on the basis of his or her protected status
column12: and (5) “so severe
column13: pervasive
column14: and objectively offensive that it effectively bars the victim’s access to an educational opportunity or benefit.” Unless your university’s harassment code limits itself to banning a similarly extreme pattern of behavior
column15: as opposed to merely hurtful or offensive speech
column16: it is very likely unconstitutional.

column1: But I Thought That Harassment Meant Stalking …

Many people confuse the concept of “discriminatory harassment” with that of simple “harassment” as understood by the common law. When one targets speech or conduct at a specific person in order to cause severe emotional distress in that person
column2: one commits the crime of harassment. Examples of harassment might include following someone in a public place (stalking) or making persistent
column3: uninvited phone calls to that person. Speech used to harass someone enjoys no First Amendment protection. “Discriminatory harassment” and “harassment
column4: ” however
column5: are two different categories. When the concept of “discriminatory harassment” was first formulated in the 1970s
column6: its proponents borrowed a name from the existing concept of “harassment
column7: ” because one of the ways in which such discrimination can be effected is through persistent behavior. Because persistent behavior is a mark of both harassment and discriminatory harassment
column8: some behavior is in fact both harassment and discriminatory harassment
column9: but neither behavior is necessarily the other.

column1: Here
column2: again
column3: analyzing speech and acts in terms of “time
column4: place
column5: or manner” is helpful. If you repeatedly phone a student in the early morning hours to tell her you hate her
column6: that intrusion would constitute harassment. However
column7: if you phone repeatedly at those hours to say that you love her
column8: and the calls are not welcome
column9: that
column10: too
column11: is harassment
column12: despite the message of love instead of hate; what is harassing is the pervasive
column13: repeated
column14: unwelcome nature of the message at an inconvenient and disturbing hour
column15: against the will of the listener.

column1: Challenging Your University's Speech Code

The long list of defeats for unconstitutional speech codes on campus proves that a mere invocation of discriminatory harassment doctrine will not be allowed to swallow up the First Amendment on campus. Nonetheless
column2: your own college’s or university’s harassment code might say otherwise—which means that challenging your university code in court might be an option worth exploring. Challenging your school’s speech codes is an excellent way to stand up for not only your own right to free expression
column3: but also the rights of your fellow students. Students on every public university campus are legally entitled to the full protection of the First Amendment—and any denial of this right is illegal
column4: unconstitutional
column5: and a betrayal of the university’s role as a marketplace of ideas. You do not have the option of violating the law
column6: so why should your university? Besides a desire to vindicate free speech rights on campus
column7: challenging your university’s speech code requires little work from students. For more on mounting a challenge to your university’s code
column8: see FIRE’s Challenging Your College’s Speech Code
column9: available on our website at www.thefire.org.

column1: As a preliminary step
column2: however
column3: arm yourself with knowledge of Supreme Court decisions
column4: such as Davis and Hustler
column5: and with OCR’s own assertion of the obvious priority of First Amendment rights over considerations of discriminatory harassment. You well might convince a college administrator that if a unanimous Supreme Court decided that remarkably hostile speech was protected by the First Amendment (in Hustler )
column6: and if the government’s own chief enforcer
column7: OCR
column8: formally has declared that harassment must go far beyond mere expression offensive to some

column10: you well might convince such an administrator that he or she would have to defend indefensible censorship. Also
column11: you might refer to the many federal cases that have thrown out speech codes that sought to prohibit merely “offensive” language

column13: simply renaming insults “discriminatory harassment” does not overthrow the Constitution and the Bill of Rights. To fall into that grave category
column14: speech truly must be so extreme and pervasive that it genuinely deprives the victim of an equal opportunity to pursue his or her education. Such cases are rare.

column1: The Difference Between Harassment in the Workplace and Harassment on Campus
Many campus codes are based upon the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s (EEOC’s) workplace regulations
column2: which can be much too broad for a community of learning (in contrast to a community of labor). Thus
column3: communicating an unpleasant opinion to a fellow student is a perfectly appropriate part of the college learning experience and of academic freedom
column4: but it might be found inappropriate in the workplace. The dangerous application of workplace standards to an academic setting causes many difficulties for freedom of speech and academic freedom
column5: both of which are essential to education.

column1: In the employment context
column2: in order for behavior to be considered hostile environment harassment
column3: it must be either serious (“severe”) or repeated (“pervasive”). As the Supreme Court put it in a decision known as Harris v. Forklift Systems
column5: behavior that is “merely offensive” does not qualify as severe or pervasive. In the educational context
column6: the behavior
column7: to qualify as discriminatory harassment
column8: must be so severe and pervasive
column9: and so “objectively offensive
column10: ” that it “effectively bars the victim’s access to an educational opportunity or benefit
column11: ” as discussed above.

column1: These differences are of real importance

column12: ” Change correctly notes that specific guidance regarding the precise parameters of academic freedom has not been forthcoming from the high court. In the absence of such guidance
column13: courts typically use “academic freedom” as one additional legal factor or rhetorical device to be weighed with or against other constitutional doctrines
column14: such as the public employee speech rules that we discussed earlier.

column1: In fact
column2: because of the lack of guidance from the Supreme Court
column3: there remains an ongoing debate over who actually possesses the right to academic freedom—students
column4: professors
column5: and/or the university itself. It is wholly true
column6: of course
column7: that all universities
column8: public or private
column9: have a certain right—indeed
column10: mission—to define the curriculum and other aspects of higher education as they see fit. For example
column11: in the case of Lovelace v. Southeastern Massachusetts University (1986)
column12: the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit noted that “[M]atters such as course content
column13: homework load
column14: and grading policies are core university concerns.” And in Sweezy v. New Hampshire (1957)
column15: Justice Felix Frankfurter’s concurring opinion noted the “four essential freedoms of a university—to determine for itself on academic grounds who may teach
column16: what may be taught
column17: how it shall be taught
column18: and who may be admitted to study.” But faculty and students may legitimately claim a right to academic freedom
column19: as well.

column1: In general
column2: to prevail on a First Amendment academic freedom claim
column3: students and professors must usually join academic freedom with another claim based on some other constitutional doctrine. It is important to keep in mind that when a university obstructs academic freedom
column4: it usually has violated some other constitutional right (or rights)
column5: so that joining these claims is not usually a difficult task. In addition
column6: as a practical matter
column7: academic freedom arguments exercise a strong power in university communities
column8: which tend to think of themselves as devoted to this value (whether such a self-image is accurate or not). On more than one occasion
column9: FIRE has persuaded administrators to lift speech restrictions or end oppressive practices by arguing that those policies or behaviors impair academic freedom. At a time when officials are all too ready to turn their backs on the First Amendment
column10: the concept of academic freedom can still have an enormous effect on them. Even the most totalitarian professors and administrators will often pay lip service to academic freedom
column11: and they can be called to task and
column12: indeed
column13: shamed when their actions do not match their words.

column1: Also
column2: universities may give students and faculty legal rights to academic freedom when they enact policies guaranteeing academic freedom. Many campuses have adopted the 1940 Statement of Principles on Academic Freedom and Tenure
column3: issued jointly by the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) and the Association of American Colleges and Universities. This statement
column4: generally known as “the AAUP Guidelines
column5: ” reflects widely shared professional norms within the academic community. Such norms
column6: when adopted by universities
column7: are almost always legally binding—a contract
column8: in effect—thereby making academic freedom the legal right of faculty members and students (whose right to reasoned dissent in a classroom
column9: without penalty
column10: is also guaranteed by the Guidelines). As a general rule
column11: such academic freedom policies relate to speech in the classroom or to areas of academic study. If you believe that your classroom speech is being stifled or if your scholarly efforts are being suppressed
column12: you immediately should check your student handbook or the university website for an academic freedom policy. Many mistakenly believe that only faculty members
column13: or only tenured faculty
column14: are protected strongly by campus academic freedom policies. Since
column15: as noted
column16: the AAUP policies apply to students also
column17: you would do well to assert academic freedom whenever censorship looms.

column1: Given the threat to faculty speech presented by courts’ interpretations of Garcetti
column2: as discussed above
column3: it is important to note that many professors
column4: through faculty governance bodies
column5: are taking action to protect academic freedom as a matter of policy at their institutions. In fact
column6: a faculty member’s best protection from restrictions on his or her classroom speech may come not from the First Amendment
column7: but from the school’s individual academic freedom policy. At the University of Minnesota
column8: for example
column9: faculty members passed a provision in response to Garcetti asserting their commitment to “the freedom to discuss all relevant matters in the classroom
column10: to explore all avenues of scholarship
column11: research
column12: and creative expression
column13: and to speak or write without institutional discipline or restraint on matters of public concern as well as on matters related to professional duties and the functioning of the university.” The University of Michigan
column14: the University of Wisconsin
column15: and others have passed similar policy changes in an attempt to ensure academic freedom has real meaning on campus.

column1: However
column2: even before Garcetti
column3: faculty speech posed particularly knotty questions for courts
column4: as evidenced by two cases from the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit. In the first case
column5: Bonnell v. Lorenzo (2001)
column6: the Sixth Circuit upheld a college’s discipline of a professor who
column7: in the college administration’s view
column8: used sexually offensive language in the classroom
column9: and who published a satirical “apology” for his actions. (According to the professor
column10: he used the language to show his students how “chauvinism” marginalized women.) Here
column11: the court ruled that because Bonnell’s “offensive” classroom speech was not related to the topic of his course
column12: it was not constitutionally protected. Further
column13: it ruled that while the satirical apology (which addressed the issue of sexual harassment) related to matters of public concern
column14: the school’s interests in maintaining a learning environment free of sexual harassment outweighed the professor’s interests in free speech and academic freedom.

column1: Just months after Bonnell
column2: however
column3: the same court decided the case of Hardy v. Jefferson Community College (2001). Here
column4: the court ruled that a college could not terminate a professor for using offensive language about women and minorities when such language was “germane” to the subject matter of the class. (Hardy had used the language to help his students examine how language can be used to “marginalize” women and minorities.) In Hardy
column5: the court applied the principles of academic freedom to decide that
column6: in this case
column7: college administrators even could be held liable for punishing a professor’s allegedly “offensive” language during class. As reasonable academic officials
column8: the court found
column9: they “should have known” that a professor’s speech
column10: when germane to the subject material of a class and when advancing a legitimate academic purpose
column11: is always protected by the First Amendment.

column1: Cases like these
column2: taken together
column3: can lead to uncertainty and confusion. In Hardy
column4: so-called offensive language was considered “germane” to classroom discussions and is therefore constitutionally protected. In Bonnell
column5: similarly offensive language was considered a “deliberate superfluous attack on a captive audience.” Within the scope of the holdings of other courts
column6: however
column7: Bonnell appears aberrational. In cases such as Cohen v. San Bernardino Valley College (1996)
column8: courts have held that speech policies similar to those used to discipline the professor in Bonnell were void because they were too vague and because the policies unconstitutionally restricted a teacher’s right to free speech and academic freedom in the classroom. Again
column9: it might well take a Supreme Court decision to resolve the differences between the two sets of views
column10: particularly against the backdrop of Garcetti ’s expansion of the government’s power as an employer.

column1: One lesson that may be drawn from these seemingly conflicting cases
column2: however
column3: is that when it comes to determining the parameters of a professor’s right to academic freedom
column4: context matters . The standard of what language is “germane” to the classroom will always remain a matter of contention and must be decided on a case-by-case basis.

column1: Despite all the confusion
column2: the principles of academic freedom serve to emphasize the particular importance of giving broad free speech rights to the academic environment. As eminent historian C. Vann Woodward wrote in the Report of the Committee on Freedom of Expression at Yale
column3: commissioned by Yale University in 1975: “The primary function of a university is to discover and disseminate knowledge by means of research and teaching. To fulfill this function a free interchange of ideas is necessary not only within its walls but with the world beyond as well. It follows that the university must do everything possible to ensure within it the fullest degree of intellectual freedom.”

column1: Defamation (Libel and Slander)
Defamation is among the most misunderstood areas of First Amendment law. During intense discussion of political or social issues (and especially during discussions of controversial personalities)
column2: people throw around allegations of libel and slander thoughtlessly and imprecisely—particularly on campus. For example
column3: student newspapers are often intimidated into adjusting or even killing stories by threats of libel suits. Compounding the problem
column4: allegations of slander and libel are particularly problematic on campus because college administrators are ill-suited to evaluate and police such charges. As a result
column5: FIRE strongly believes that colleges and universities have no business policing or punishing student speech for defamation. However
column6: given the frequency of the accusations and the consequences to free speech of ignorance and fear in these matters
column7: it is critical that students—and
column8: most importantly
column9: student journalists—have a basic understanding of a doctrine that should have
column10: in fact
column11: little impact on the free marketplace of ideas.

column1: Defamation is a false communication that harms individuals’ reputations
column2: causes the general public to hate or disrespect them
column3: or damages their business or employment. A respected legal definition of defamation is communication that “tends so to harm the reputation of another as to lower him in the estimation of the community or to deter third persons from associating or dealing with him.” The concept of defamation includes both libel (usually
column4: written defamation) and slander (spoken defamation)
column5: although the two are frequently confused or lumped together. Libel charges generally involve a civil lawsuit brought by the alleged victim against the speaker.

column1: Laws prohibiting defamation are both very ancient and very complex—another reason college administrators should not police or punish student speech on such charges—but even a cursory summary of the law will reassure most. If you are sued in civil court for libel
column2: do not panic. Although defamation is one of the most frequently made claims in law
column3: it is also one of the most frequently dismissed. Many college students profoundly misunderstand and underestimate how difficult it is
column4: in fact
column5: to win a defamation case. Even so
column6: if you find yourself accused of defamation
column7: you certainly may wish to consult with a lawyer to determine if you are at any risk of liability.

column1: In general
column2: you can speak passionately about individuals and issues without fear of a defamation lawsuit. There are indeed
column3: however
column4: some kinds of statements that carry particular risk
column5: such as falsely accusing someone of having a disease or of being promiscuous; falsely saying that someone is incompetent at his or her job; or falsely stating that someone committed a serious crime
column6: including a sexual offense. As always
column7: some amount of common sense and basic moral judgment are good rules of thumb. If you wrote an article claiming that “John is a pedophile” when you knew this to be a lie or even without any reasonable grounds for believing it to be true
column8: you should not be surprised to find yourself in serious legal difficulty.

column1: The precise legal elements of defamation vary from state to state
column2: but the offense must always be premised on a false and derogatory statement. (If a statement is true
column3: it is not defamatory. Proving the truth of your statement
column4: of course
column5: can sometimes be difficult.)

column1: Furthermore
column2: to be defamatory
column3: a statement must be an assertion of fact (rather than mere opinion) and capable of being proven false . A statement of opinion
column4: by itself
column5: cannot be defamation. For example
column6: saying that “Alex is a jerk” would not be defamation. This would not be understood by any reasonable listener to be anything other than opinion. Statements that are so hyperbolic or exaggerated that no one could consider them to be statements of fact are also protected (for instance
column7: “Alex has the charm of a rattlesnake”). Because of these requirements
column8: everyday insults
column9: epithets
column10: and sharp-edged parody are usually not considered defamatory. However
column11: writing that “Alex is a murderer” could well be libel
column12: because the statement seems to be communicating a factual allegation. It is important to note that while “pure” opinions are protected
column13: you still may be held liable if you make a factual statement after first stating “in my opinion.” Since the Supreme Court case of Milkovich v. Lorain Journal Co. (1990)
column14: it has been clear that just adding “ in my opinion ” to the false statement “Alex walked up to Liam and shot him” will not stop a statement from being defamatory. Again
column15: common sense is not a bad first guide in all of this.

column1: In addition to being false
column2: the statement
column3: to be defamatory
column4: must identify its victim by naming or reasonably implicating the person allegedly defamed. For example
column5: if you were to say falsely that “the whole chess club” is involved in a real crime
column6: and there were only a few people in the chess club
column7: each of them would likely have a legal claim against you.

column1: Usually
column2: state laws also require the statement to be published (literally
column3: made public or announced) before it can be deemed defamatory. However
column4: the common legal definition of “published” in this context requires only that the allegedly defamatory statement be communicated to the target and at least one other person. While this is a fairly easy definition of publication to meet
column5: it does keep exclusively private communications between two people from being defamatory. If you say something privately to the person you scorn
column6: it is not defamatory in any legal sense.

column1: States require that the plaintiff (the individual claiming to be defamed) prove at least some fault on the part of the publisher
column2: speaker
column3: or author of the defamatory statement. Someone bringing a claim must show that you were
column4: at the very least
column5: careless in making the defamatory statement. If you were very careful in checking all your sources before making a supposedly defamatory statement
column6: then
column7: in all probability
column8: you will not be found liable
column9: even if for some reason your statement turned out to be false.

column1: Finally
column2: it is necessary that the plaintiff prove that he or she was actually harmed by the statement. An important misconception about defamation is that the offense comes from the emotional hurt the defamation causes. That is not the case. The reason behind laws against defamation is not to protect individuals from feeling bad
column3: but to prevent unjust damage to their reputations
column4: livelihoods
column5: or both . Such harm
column6: to be defamatory
column7: must have a real negative impact on their lives. In many libel cases
column8: the supposedly defamed plaintiffs must show that their careers or finances suffered from the statement. Defamation is not based solely on the emotional distress felt by the target. In other words
column9: defamation is about objective harm
column10: not subjective hurt .

column1: It is worth repeating that FIRE strongly believes that
column2: generally speaking
column3: colleges and universities have no business prosecuting claims of defamation. The doctrine is simply too complex for college administrators to navigate in a fair and just way.

column1: Constitutional Limits on Defamation Claims
Because the First Amendment would be virtually meaningless if we could never criticize anyone
column2: especially a public figure
column3: without feeling exposed to financial ruin from a libel suit
column4: there are very strong constitutional limitations on defamation lawsuits. The most important and best known protections exist precisely to make certain that defamation is not used to punish people for participating in socially important debate
column5: discussion
column6: and expression.

column1: First
column2: there is the protection given to criticism of public figures. The landmark Supreme Court opinion in New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) ruled that the status of the person claiming to be defamed—is that individual a “public” or a “private” figure?—is one of the most important factors in a defamation case. Because the area of defamation law dealing with “public” or “private” status is complex
column3: the best way to understand the law here is to analyze how it applies to the kinds of people discussed and to the kinds of statements that are made.

column1: Categories of People
Public Officials and Public Figures. To preserve a society in which citizens are free to criticize those who hold and have held power
column2: the law makes it quite difficult for public officials and public figures to sue someone successfully for defamation. Public officials would include not only the President of the United States
column3: congressmen
column4: and governors
column5: but also
column6: almost certainly
column7: the president of your university. Public figures need not be governmental officials
column8: but also can include celebrities or others who have achieved a high degree of public notoriety. The singer Beyoncé Knowles
column9: for example
column10: would be what the law calls an “all-purpose public figure
column11: ” a person who is so well known that virtually everything about him or her is considered to be of public interest.

column1: Some individuals can be what the courts define as “limited purpose public figures.” That is to say
column2: they are so involved in certain topics or issues that they are considered public figures on that limited topic. On other issues
column3: however
column4: they are treated as private citizens. Whether your professor is a public figure is not always clear
column5: but some professors are such celebrities on some topics that they may be considered public figures in those areas of expertise or fame. If someone appears on television and radio to discuss certain issues
column6: for example
column7: or writes books on certain subjects
column8: then
column9: with regard to those topics
column10: he or she is almost certainly
column11: at the least
column12: a “limited purpose public figure.” Also
column13: the publication’s audience is an important contextual consideration here; for the purpose of a campus newspaper
column14: a well-known administrator or faculty member may qualify as a public figure
column15: even if he or she would not be considered as such outside of campus.

column1: It is extremely difficult for a public figure or a limited purpose public figure to win a defamation suit. A public figure basically would have to prove that a newspaper or individual not only made false statements
column2: but also knew
column3: or unmistakably should have known
column4: that the statements were false when made. In other words
column5: the Constitution allows public figures to recover for damages in defamation cases only when the harm is caused either by intentional falsehoods or by falsehoods resulting from what the courts call “a reckless disregard for the truth.” It is not enough for public figures who sue for defamation to prove that you were merely careless ; instead
column6: they would have to prove either that you lied knowingly or that you showed a wild disregard for the truth in saying what you said.

column1: Private Persons. Anyone who is not a public figure or official is considered a “private person” in defamation law. This category includes the great majority of citizens
column2: and it almost certainly includes most students
column3: faculty
column4: staff
column5: and ordinary administrators at a public or private university. It is easier to be successfully sued for defaming a private person than a public figure. Private figures generally do not have to prove that you knew your defamatory statements were false when you made them. In other words
column6: you can be guilty of defamation even if you were not intentionally lying about the plaintiff.

column1: Categories of Statements
Statements on Matters of Public Concern . As a general rule
column2: a statement on a topic that affects the public’s welfare is a statement that has a substantial impact on a substantial number of individuals. Examples of such statements in the educational setting would include a widespread cheating scandal
column3: the resignation of a prominent administrator
column4: tuition hikes
column5: and a controversial decision to fire a professor. Much like statements regarding public figures
column6: statements on topics that concern public welfare enjoy a substantially high level of constitutional protection. The reason is obvious: We want to encourage fairly unfettered discourse and debate on subjects of substantial public importance. It is in society’s deepest interest not to chill such discussion.

column1: Statements on Purely Personal Matters. The definition of a “personal matter” is largely an issue of common sense. Discussions of another person’s romantic relationships
column2: divorce
column3: pregnancies
column4: illnesses
column5: personal finances
column6: and so on
column7: all would be matters of purely personal concern. False and injurious comments about such personal matters (but only the personal concerns of private rather than public figures) enjoy the least constitutional protection in defamation law.

column1: Finally
column2: it is important to note that the most critical defense to a defamation suit is
column3: quite simply
column4: the truth . If you can prove that what you are saying is true
column5: you have no legal consequences to fear from a defamation claim. (It is important to note that the burden of proving falsity will fall on the individual alleging defamation
column6: except in cases involving the personal matters of private parties
column7: in which damages may be available even for plaintiffs who do not prove falsity.) While other defenses to defamation may be available (such as an argument that the defamed individual consented to publication or that the defamatory comments are privileged in some way)
column8: none of those defenses has as much legal power as the truth. You are most likely to be found guilty of defamation if someone can prove that you knew the defamatory allegation you made was false when you made it
column9: or that you intentionally avoided finding out the truth. You are virtually certain to escape liability if you are telling the truth and can prove that it is the truth. In the eyes of the law
column10: honesty really is the best policy.

column1: Online Speech: The First Amendment in the Internet Age
Given the incredible progression of technological advancement
column2: students today enjoy an unprecedented number of ways to express themselves—faster
column3: cheaper
column4: and simpler than ever before. The ubiquity of lightning-fast high-speed internet connections at today’s universities
column5: coupled with the powerful laptops
column6: tablets
column7: and smartphones carried by today’s students
column8: means that students enjoy the ability to communicate with the world around them in thrilling new ways
column9: publishing their words far across the digital world at the press of a button. It is no exaggeration to classify this sea change in global communication as a true technological revolution
column10: and one that should excite any lover of ideas.

column1: But with ever-more robust means of self-expression at their fingertips
column2: students are also increasingly discovering a disappointing truth: Censorship is a persistent and tenacious phenomenon. Since FIRE’s founding in 1999
column3: the number of cases involving the censorship of online student expression has risen annually at an extraordinary rate. This is perhaps unsurprising
column4: if also discouraging and of course unwarranted. Because while today’s wired students enjoy email
column5: social networking
column6: blogs
column7: and the wide world of online communication to talk to one another in new ways
column8: the actual content of student speech remains largely unchanged. Just like their parents and grandparents
column9: today’s students will express themselves in passionate and provocative ways that will elicit strong responses from certain audiences. (And often
column10: such responses are precisely the speaker’s intent!) Accordingly
column11: then
column12: some students will believe they enjoy an illusory right “not to be offended
column13: ” and some administrators will agree. Similarly
column14: some student speech will prove too provocative for an administrator
column15: who will seek to silence this unwanted and inconvenient voice. The impulse to censor surely dates back to the beginning of humankind’s ability to express itself.

column1: Furthermore
column2: much online communication
column3: particularly blogs and social networking sites
column4: is far more visible to the general public than previous modes of student expression. Whereas before
column5: a conversation between two students might have taken place on a walk across the campus green
column6: it now may be relocated to Twitter
column7: where it may be available for consumption by a far wider audience. An impassioned debate between students may previously have centered in a dorm room; today
column8: it may be conducted via a series of heated blog posts. The peril in this new visibility lies in the fact that sometimes the tone
column9: subject matter
column10: or language of college discussions is offensive to others both on and off campus. Moreover
column11: the new visibility of online speech may expose student dialogue to audiences for whom it was not intended
column12: as administrators eavesdrop on previously private student speech.

column1: It is this new access to student speech that likely prompts the increased instances of censorship of online speech. But as FIRE President Greg Lukianoff and Director of Legal and Public Advocacy Will Creeley noted in a 2011 Charleston Law Review article entitled New Media
column2: Old Principles
column3: “it is crucial that administrators remember that no matter the means of the expression
column4: the core principles guiding our understanding of what speech is and is not protected remain unchanged.” Lukianoff and Creeley wrote:

column1: The First Amendment has weathered technological revolutions before
column2: and it will do so again. For the most part
column3: the legal tests we employ to ascertain whether speech enjoys First Amendment protection do not rely on the medium in which the expression occurs. The exacting definition of peer-on-peer harassment remains the same
column4: whether the speech takes place online or on the campus green; the legal test for incitement still requires the satisfaction of the same elements
column5: whether the expression at issue is visible on a screen or heard on the way to class. While the media may be new
column6: the speech—and how we evaluate it—is not.

column1: Further
column2: the new visibility of speech offers opportunities for increased understanding and tolerance of differing viewpoints and different ways of speaking to one another. This is a significant development. In the first years following FIRE’s founding in 1999
column3: it was possible to believe that campus administrators consistently overreacted to student speech because they were simply not familiar with the way students actually talk to each other in private: using slang
column4: vulgarity
column5: insults intended to be affectionate
column6: multiple levels of sarcasm and irony
column7: and jokes sometimes intended to mean the exact opposite of what a plain reading might indicate. Now
column8: with an ocean of student speech published on Facebook and Twitter
column9: administrators are hard-pressed to avoid a greater level of familiarity with the actual nature of student speech. Administrators need to realize that jokes are jokes
column10: and unfunny
column11: would-be collegiate comedians do not enjoy any less First Amendment protection than the rest of us. It can reasonably be hoped that electronic media and the sheer volume and diversity of the communications to which it provides access and insight will eventually encourage college administrators to drop attempts to police student speech—if not due to a newfound respect for free speech
column12: then out of a recognition of the utter futility of the enterprise.

column1: As once private speech becomes increasingly public online
column2: we must allow our social expectations to evolve to accommodate viewpoints and ways of speaking that
column3: while not our own
column4: are nevertheless protected by the First Amendment. By doing so
column5: we can begin to resolve the current tension regarding online speech on campus.

column1: FROM LAW BOOKS AND THEORIES TO PRACTICE: FREE SPEECH ON TODAY’S CAMPUSES
Up to this point
column2: we have buried you
column3: we fear
column4: in an avalanche of legal doctrines and arguments. The fact is that First Amendment law is a complex maze that even lawyers find difficult to navigate. It is very important
column5: therefore
column6: for any comprehensive free speech Guide to demonstrate how the law is applied in practice . The scenarios that follow are based on real cases that FIRE has confronted—and continues to confront—in its ongoing battle for free speech on campus.

column1: In exploring the following scenarios
column2: remember that restrictions on free expression take many forms. In addition to more easily recognized instances of pure censorship
column3: you may encounter many other abridgements on your right to free speech: official “investigations” launched into controversial
column4: dissenting
column5: or simply unpopular speech; the confiscation of newspapers
column6: flyers
column7: or other printed materials; the imposition of prohibitively expensive security fees on student groups wishing to bring a controversial speaker to campus; “probation” periods or warnings about future punishment for speech; and other such threats. Even if a student speaker is not ultimately punished for his or her speech
column8: months of “informal” investigations or other “unofficial” threats constitute punishment in and of themselves
column9: creating an impermissible “chilling effect” on campus speech and dissuading students from exercising their right to free expression. After all
column10: if every time a student voiced an opinion
column11: they risked being hauled into the Dean’s office or being subjected to an official investigation
column12: most students would not bother taking the risk. You should never allow administrators to excuse such illiberal actions by claiming that no “official” action was ever taken. As a rule of thumb
column13: remember that any use of official power to discourage free speech is deeply problematic at a public institution or a private institution that promises the right to freedom of expression.

column1: 1.Your College Enacts (or Considers Enacting) a Policy That Bans “Offensive” or “Hurtful” Speech
SCENARIO: The student government of your university is considering enacting rules that would ban “offensive” speech
column2: or speech that “demeans
column3: ” “provokes
column4: ” or “subordinates” any member of a particular group. Or
column5: perhaps
column6: it is trying to redefine punishable “fighting words” as any speech that “stigmatizes” a student on the basis of race or gender. Or
column7: perhaps
column8: the administration is passing new rules that require all student speech to be “civil.” Would this be allowable at a public university? How about a private university? What if your school already has rules that punish this sort of speech?

column1: What is a Speech Code?
FIRE defines a speech code as any campus regulation that punishes
column2: forbids
column3: heavily regulates
column4: or restricts a substantial amount of protected speech. While it would be helpful for purposes of identification (and more honest) if universities listed their speech restrictions in a section of the student handbook called “OUR SPEECH CODE
column5: ” almost all universities disguise their speech restrictions
column6: if only for public relations purposes. Speech codes may come in the form of highly restrictive “speech zone” policies
column7: email policies that ban “offensive” communication
column8: diversity statements that include provisions that punish people who engage in “intolerant expression” or “acts of intolerance
column9: ” and
column10: of course
column11: the ever-present “harassment policies” aimed at “hurtful” or “offensive” viewpoints and words.

column1: We have seen some truly laughable codes over the past twelve years here at FIRE. For example
column2: Drexel University’s former harassment policy banned “inconsiderate jokes” and “inappropriately directed laughter.” Mansfield University of Pennsylvania bans any behavior that would “diminish [another student’s] self-esteem” or their “striving for competence.” The University of Florida lists “humor and jokes about sex that denigrate a gender” as an example of actionable sexual harassment
column3: and Illinois State University bans “discussions about sexual activity.” Harvard University reserves the right to punish students for “grave disrespect for the dignity of others.”

column1: It is important to remember that simply calling a restriction on student speech something else does not alleviate the damage it does to campus discourse. For example
column2: a university can and should ban true harassment or threats
column3: but a code that calls itself a “harassment code” does not thereby magically free itself from its obligations to free speech and academic freedom. The reality
column4: not the name
column5: determines the nature of these things. Know your rights.

column1: What if Your University is Considering a Speech Code?
Rules that punish merely “offensive” speech are plainly unconstitutional at public colleges and universities. Indeed
column2: as the courts frequently remind us
column3: the First Amendment is most important for its role in protecting speech that others find offensive or dangerous. Popular and pleasant speech rarely needs special protection
column4: because it is almost never the target of censors. In an exceptional string of victories dating back more than two decades
column5: courts have consistently and repeatedly struck down speech codes when challenged. Typically
column6: these unconstitutional speech codes characterized offensive speech as a form of harassment
column7: analogous to sexual harassment
column8: or as fighting words
column9: or as some combination of these two justifications for curtailing expression. These codes usually dealt specifically with speech that concerned race
column10: gender
column11: sexual orientation
column12: or a number of other protected categories. (In the University of Michigan case
column13: special protection was extended to “race
column14: ethnicity
column15: religion
column16: sex
column17: sexual orientation
column18: creed
column19: national origin
column20: ancestry
column21: age
column22: marital status
column23: handicap or Vietnam-era veteran status
column24: ” leaving someone trying to avoid these categories in quite a bind.) No matter how these policies were drawn or how hard the authors of these speech codes tried to make them look as if they applied only to speech that was already unprotected

column1: The three reasons that the courts consistently gave for overturning these policies were that they were vague
column2: they were overbroad
column3: and they discriminated on the basis of viewpoint (see the earlier discussions of vagueness
column4: overbreadth
column5: and viewpoint discrimination). For example
column6: because it is unclear what sort of speech “stigmatizes on the basis of creed
column7: ” a code would be unconstitutionally vague. Because speech that may “demean” someone on the basis of sex may include unmistakably protected speech (for example
column8: “men never ask for directions”; “women make better parents”; “women shouldn’t be allowed to serve in combat roles”; or even “I just don’t think that men deserve the right to vote”; and so forth)
column9: it would be overbroad. Also
