column10: because these codes were typically aimed at speech with a point of view about race
column11: gender
column12: or sexual orientation (usually they were aimed at speech that was in some way hostile to the “university’s values” on these subjects)
column13: they were impermissible viewpoint-based restrictions. A rule that required students to be “civil” in their discourse also would likely be unconstitutionally vague and overbroad
column14: and it would almost certainly be applied in an unconstitutionally viewpoint-discriminatory way.

column1: Whether a private university may legally enact a speech code depends on several factors. First
column2: as discussed above
column3: some states have rules that require private universities to give free speech rights to their students
column4: as was the case when Stanford University’s speech code was struck down in 1995. A second consideration is how the university promotes itself. If a private university not in a state providing speech protections to students says prominently in its promotional literature that it values “community standards” above all other rights and concerns
column5: it could legally enforce a speech code based on these advertised standards. If
column6: however
column7: a private university promotes itself as a place that provides the greatest possible free speech rights to its students
column8: but it then tries to forbid speech that may be offensive to some
column9: it is likely to be violating its contract with its students and therefore committing breach of contract
column10: if not outright fraud. A student in this situation would have a fairly powerful claim against his or her school
column11: especially if contract law in that state takes seriously such pacts between school and student.

column1: Even when a private university has the legal right to pass a speech code
column2: you should force it to consider seriously whether it is wise to do so. Does Harvard University
column3: for example
column4: truly want to provide (or be known to provide) less free speech than the local public community college? When fighting a speech code
column5: remind your university that First Amendment law is not simply a collection of inconvenient regulations
column6: but a free people’s collective wisdom on expressive liberty. Even if your school is not legally bound by the Constitution
column7: it should recognize that the broad protections and carefully chosen limitations of the First Amendment may be the best “speech code” for any institution of higher education. You have tremendous moral authority when you talk in terms of the university’s solemn obligation to protect freedom of inquiry and discourse. Take advantage of that authority. Take the debate public. As Justice Brandeis correctly observed
column8: sunlight is the best disinfectant.

column1: What if Your University Already has a Speech Code (As it probably does)?
Sadly
column2: hundreds of American colleges and universities already have speech codes
column3: even though these codes generally violate the Constitution
column4: state law
column5: or their own stated policies. Indeed
column6: FIRE’s most recent survey of campus speech codes
column7: Spotlight on Speech Codes 2012: The State of Free Speech on Our Nation’s Campuses
column8: found that 65 percent of the 392 colleges and universities analyzed maintain policies that seriously infringe upon students’ free speech rights. We recommend that you investigate your university’s policies to see if you have a speech code. (FIRE lists and rates the speech policies maintained by hundreds of our nation’s colleges and universities at www.thefire.org/spotlight .)

column1: Remember
column2: the speech code may be part of your university’s code of misconduct
column3: or be hidden in the language of the sexual or racial harassment policies
column4: or located in any number of places in your student code. The bottom line is that if the policy applies to speech and goes beyond the narrow permissible limitations on protected speech outlined in this Guide
column5: it likely is an unconstitutional speech code on public campuses and a violation of contractual promises on private campuses. Often
column6: prosecutions based on these codes occur behind closed doors
column7: with no publicity
column8: with the frightened respondent accepting a demeaning plea bargain in order to avoid severe punishment. The fact that you never have heard of such a prosecution does not mean that speech is not punished on your campus. Investigate
column9: and then act on behalf of freedom. Once administrations are aware that you know that they have a speech code
column10: they will have to weigh the value of the code versus the very real possibility the courts will force them to eliminate or narrow it or that public opinion will shame them for their betrayal of American values.

column1: While it is vital to know the law and use it to defend your rights
column2: most of these battles are won in the field of debate and public persuasion. You should challenge those students and faculty who defend the speech codes
column3: who claim that they are necessary to protect minority
column4: female
column5: or homosexual students. You should argue that sheltering students from speech that might offend them is patronizing and paternalistic. No one who claims that groups of students are too weak to live with the Bill of Rights or with freedom is their friend. You should argue that repression results only in people hiding their real attitudes. If prejudice
column6: bigotry
column7: or ignorance exists
column8: it is far better to know how people actually think
column9: to discuss such things
column10: and to reply appropriately
column11: rather than to force such things underground
column12: where they only fester and worsen. If you are hated by someone
column13: it is better (and safer) to know who hates you and why. It is counterproductive to force educable human beings to disguise their true beliefs and feelings. It is counterproductive to create a climate in which students are afraid to speak frankly and freely with one another. Challenge the administration on the university’s motivation for passing these speech codes. Do such restrictions of liberty serve the educational development of students and the search for truth
column14: or do they merely give administrators the appearance of peace and quiet at the expense of real progress and candor? Is the administration simply interested in “quiet on its watch” rather than in real education and honest human interaction? Remind administrators that pain and offense—the inevitable by-product of having one’s fundamental beliefs challenged—is a vital part of the educational process
column15: and that if students graduate without ever having to evaluate their positions on fundamental principles
column16: then the university has failed them. Finally
column17: for those who are not interested in principled arguments
column18: remind them that history shows us that the censors of one generation are the censored of the next. Everyone should defend free speech out of self-interest
column19: if for nothing else. In any democracy
column20: as a result of elections
column21: the pendulum always swings. What is sauce for the goose soon becomes sauce for the gander. Those in power should value liberty not only for its own sake
column22: but for their own. Freedom of speech is a precious thing. It is indispensable to our living decently
column23: peacefully
column24: and fairly with each other. It also is indispensable to protecting all of us from abuses of arbitrary power.

column1: Finally
column2: you may run into administrators who reply to criticism of the speech code by assuring you that “it is never enforced.” Even if you believe this is true (which you should by no means take for granted
column3: since universities often actively conceal such proceedings)
column4: the fact that it is not enforced is irrelevant. A law on the books that is hostile to speech would still be void for vagueness and overbreadth even if it were not ordinarily enforced. Even if a campus has never enforced its speech code
column5: the code remains a palpable and harmful form of coercion. As long as the policy exists
column6: the threat of enforcement remains real and can influence how people speak and act. Indeed
column7: it may well be that the very existence of the code has successfully deterred a certain level of vigorous discussion and argument. In First Amendment law
column8: this is known as a “chilling effect”: By having these codes in student handbooks
column9: administrators can prevent most of the speech they seek to censor just by disseminating the policy. When students see what the administration bans—or even if they are unsure
column10: because of the breadth or vagueness of the definitions—they will play it safe and avoid engaging in speech that
column11: even though constitutionally protected
column12: may offend a student or a disciplinary board. Under such circumstances
column13: students will
column14: more often than not
column15: censor themselves. The law wisely holds that these sorts of rules unconstitutionally chill speech
column16: stopping debate before it starts
column17: by forcing individuals to wonder whether or not they can be punished for speech before they open their mouths.

column1: Just as harmfully
column2: the very existence of speech codes on campus misinforms students about the extent of their right to freedom of expression. Whether or not a speech code is ever enforced
column3: the fact of its being on the school’s books signals to students that freedom of speech may be limited. Allowing the dissemination of such misinformation is sharply at odds with our traditional understanding of the role of the university as the marketplace of ideas. There is no benefit to higher education to be gained by deceiving students into thinking that they enjoy fewer rights than they actually do. Indeed
column4: such misinformation does great harm to our modern liberal democracy
column5: which relies on an engaged
column6: informed citizenry discussing the ideas of the day.

column1: Finally
column2: the “unenforced” code is there for moments of crisis
column3: which is precisely when rights and liberty have the most need of protection. At such moments of crisis
column4: discussion of speech codes becomes least rational and least principled. Now is the time to ensure the state of freedom on your campus.

column1: 2. Abuse of Hostile Environment Law: Tufts University and The Primary Source
SCENARIO: Your school newspaper
column2: on its humor page
column3: runs a joke (along with dozens of other
column4: unrelated jokes) that makes fun of the leader of the student labor association for wearing tight clothes. The next day
column5: you find that you and your paper have been charged with sexual harassment for running the joke and that your paper is threatened with loss of funding. Can the school do this?

column1: This scenario actually happened at Tufts University to a conservative student newspaper called The Primary Source . The paper published three remarks in its humor pages ridiculing the appearance and dress of female members of another student group that the paper routinely opposed. FIRE became involved when one of the mocked students brought sexual harassment charges against the paper
column2: and the paper was threatened with being shut down.

column1: This case is important because even though Tufts is a private university not bound by the First Amendment
column2: it still was not willing to deviate so starkly from First Amendment principles in order to punish student speech once the case was brought to public attention. Tufts originally claimed (and possibly sincerely believed) that its enforcement of its sexual harassment policy in this case was required by federal law. When FIRE wrote to Tufts
column3: it made the obvious and telling point that federal law cannot compel any institution to violate rights protected by the Constitution.

column1: FIRE further argued that: 1) The Primary Source was engaging in what would be clearly protected speech in the larger society; 2) this use of a sexual harassment rationale not only conflicted with the actual law
column2: but also trivialized the real offense of sexual harassment; 3) the threats against the paper constituted an attack on parody and satire
column3: time-honored traditions that are constitutionally protected in American society; 4) such a broad interpretation of sexual harassment law could potentially be used to ban all speech at the university
column4: and such a vague rule would prevent students from voicing any controversial opinions; 5) Tufts was demonstrating an intolerable double standard in its application of this overbroad policy only to this instance of offensive speech; and 6) the University would be publicly humiliated if it became widely known that Tufts was shutting down student newspapers for printing jokes.

column1: Shortly after receiving FIRE’s letter
column2: Tufts found The Primary Source innocent of all these charges.

column1: 3. Libel: University of North Carolina Wilmington
SCENARIO: A fellow student sends out an email diatribe that angers you
column2: and you respond with an email that calls the student’s communication “bigoted and unintelligent.” The student declares that she is going to sue you for libel. Can she win?

column1: A similar scenario took place at the University of North Carolina Wilmington. FIRE became involved when a student accused a professor of libel for calling a political message that she sent out widely by mail “undeserving of serious consideration
column2: ” among other critical statements. While the law of libel is complex
column3: the professor’s statement was clearly not defamatory. First
column4: to be libelous
column5: the statement must be a provably false allegation of fact. This means that it must allege something “objective
column6: ” something that could be established through facts. (For example
column7: falsely stating that someone committed a crime—“Jim set fire to the dormitory”—could be libel. Merely giving your subjective opinion of someone
column8: however—“Jim is a jerk” or “Jim is ugly”—is not libel.) Furthermore
column9: the fact that the professor’s criticism was directed at the content of what the student said
column10: and not at the student
column11: puts it well within the realm of protected speech. When an allegation is not simply a matter of opinion
column12: then truth
column13: of course
column14: is an absolute defense against a charge of libel. Libel is one of the most common charges that plaintiffs file
column15: and one of the most likely to fail. If you engage in speech about matters of public concern and are accused of libel
column16: never simply assume that your accuser has a legitimate claim against you.

column1: 4. Compelled Speech: Forcing Students to Utter Beliefs
SCENARIO: As an incoming freshman living in a university residence hall
column2: you discover that your university requires residents to attend mandatory “training” meetings with resident advisors. At these events
column3: residents are required to submit to intensive
column4: intrusive questioning about their own personal experiences and beliefs
column5: and are taught that certain beliefs are correct and necessary. Can the university do this?

column1: Shockingly
column2: this scenario actually occurred at the University of Delaware
column3: which in 2007 subjected the nearly 7
column4: 000 students living in its residence halls to just such an invasive program of ideological reeducation. Referred to in the university’s own program materials as a “treatment” for students’ attitudes and beliefs
column5: the program required students to adopt specific university-approved viewpoints on a wide range of issues
column6: including politics
column7: racial relations
column8: sexuality
column9: sociology
column10: moral philosophy
column11: and environmentalism. Student beliefs were manipulated via “training” sessions
column12: one-on-one meetings
column13: and floor events conducted by resident advisors. Each resident advisor had in turn received his or her own intensive training from the university
column14: including “diversity facilitation training” at which advisors were taught to espouse highly politicized viewpoints about a wide variety of subjects
column15: and to teach their residents the same. Per university protocol
column16: resident advisors were asked to pose intensely intrusive and personal questions to their residents
column17: such as
column18: “When did you discover your sexual identity?” Students who resisted the questioning in any way or otherwise expressed discomfort were met with disapproval from their advisors
column19: who kept records on their residents’ progress.

column1: Program materials received by FIRE showed that the residence life education program sought to have students achieve “competencies” in order to gain the larger educational goal of “citizenship.” These competencies included: “Students will recognize that systemic oppression exists in our society”; “Students will recognize the benefits of dismantling systems of oppression”; and “Students will be able to utilize their knowledge of sustainability to change their daily habits and consumer mentality.” The program further pressured and even required students to take action to indicate their agreement with the university’s official ideological viewpoints
column2: including compelling students to speak on behalf of “oppressed” social groups and otherwise advocate for a “sustainable world.” Following FIRE’s public exposure of these activities in 2007
column3: University of Delaware President Patrick Harker promptly ended the program.

column1: Students encountering similar situations must remember that no public university has the power to force its own particular understanding of society’s many debates on its students under pain of punishment. No student can be required to profess certain beliefs; to do so is to cross the line into unconstitutional compelled speech or belief. Forcing citizens to mouth propositions regardless of whether they believe them is alien to a free society. In many ways
column2: it is even worse than forms of censorship that simply stop a person from saying what he or she believes. Public universities that force students to attend mandatory diversity training or “sensitivity training” sessions
column3: at which they must pledge themselves to this or that cause or attitude—or that require them to take classes in which they must make ideological statements with which they disagree—are likely violating both constitutional rights and guarantees of academic freedom. Additionally
column4: private schools that promise their students free speech or academic freedom are in stark violation of their contracts if they require such ideological loyalty and adherence to a particular orthodoxy
column5: belief system
column6: or ideology.

column1: 5. Free Speech Zones: West Virginia University
SCENARIO: Your school designates two small areas on your campus as “free speech zones”—areas where you can engage in “free speech activities
column2: ” including protests or speeches. You are “caught” handing out pamphlets outside a public meeting on your campus
column3: and the campus police tell you that you cannot be doing that outside of the free speech zone. Can your school do this?

column1: “Free speech zones” that in effect turn the rest of a campus into censorship zones are surprisingly common on American campuses
column2: and this scenario actually occurred at West Virginia University (WVU). FIRE became involved when a student group notified us that it had been prevented by campus police from handing out protest literature beyond the designated speech zone. Additionally
column3: a student was removed from a public presentation simply for being a known protester attending a meeting outside the free speech zone.

column1: FIRE wrote to the school and informed administrators that under the United States Constitution
column2: public colleges and universities are allowed to impose only reasonable time
column3: place
column4: and manner restrictions on speech
column5: and only if those restrictions are narrowly tailored and are related to a compelling state interest (usually preventing the disruption of university functions). Under these doctrines
column6: administrators may place certain legitimate limitations on events
column7: but they most surely may not quarantine all speech to two small areas on campus. As FIRE wrote
column8: “We assure you that there is nothing ‘reasonable’ about transforming ninety-nine percent of your University’s property—indeed
column9: public property—into ‘Censorship Zones.’”

column1: FIRE also pointed out that cordoning off free speech runs completely contrary to the special role of a university in a free society:
The irony of this policy is that the societal function of the university
column2: in any free society
column3: is to serve as the ultimate “Free Speech Zone.” A university serious about the search for truth should be seeking at all times to expand open discourse
column4: to foster intellectual inquiry
column5: and to engage and challenge the way people think. By limiting free speech to a tiny fraction of the campus
column6: you send the message that speech is to be feared
column7: regulated
column8: and monitored at all times. This message is utterly incompatible with a free society and stands in stark opposition to the ideals of higher education.

column1: After receiving FIRE’s letter (and after the widespread publicity that resulted when FIRE made its letter public)
column2: the school agreed to change its policies. In the end
column3: WVU eliminated its speech zones altogether
column4: allowing protest in most places throughout the campus.

column1: The situation at WVU is hardly anomalous
column2: unfortunately
column3: and many universities continue to maintain highly restrictive free speech zones. However
column4: FIRE has been very successful in challenging and defeating free speech zones across the country. We have found that quarantining free speech to a tiny section of campus is very unpopular amongst both students and the general public
column5: and that universities are often loath to defend such zones in public when confronted about their unreasonable restrictions on student speech. Valdosta State University
column6: for example
column7: abandoned its free speech zone after FIRE publicized it in a variety of ways. Until the policy revision
column8: Valdosta State had limited free expression on the entire 168-acre campus to one small stage. What’s more
column9: Valdosta State had only allowed students to use the stage between the hours of noon and 1 PM and 5 to 6 PM
column10: and even then only on weekdays—hardly the “reasonable” time
column11: place
column12: and manner restrictions permitted by law.

column1: Some schools dismantle their free speech zones only following the filing of a lawsuit. Texas Tech University
column2: for example
column3: prohibited students from expressing themselves anywhere outside of the college’s “free speech gazebo” until students filed suit and challenged the constitutionality of the policy. In ruling that the free speech zone violated student First Amendment rights
column4: the federal district court ruled that the policy must permit students to engage in expressive activity in “park areas
column5: sidewalks
column6: streets
column7: or other similar common areas … irrespective of whether the University has so designated them or not.” Similarly
column8: Tarrant County College (TX) and Citrus College (CA) both were forced to abandon their free speech zone policies following court challenges.

column1: In considering a legal challenge to the constitutionality of a public college’s or university’s speech code
column2: remember that in addition to the First Amendment
column3: your state constitution may also guarantee certain rights and protections. For answers to common questions about the mechanics of filing a challenge to a public university’s speech policies
column4: be sure to read FIRE’s Challenging Your College’s Speech Code
column5: available at www.thefire.org . Furthermore
column6: as we have mentioned throughout this Guide
column7: many state courts have held that private colleges and universities must deliver students the rights promised in student handbooks and school policies as the fulfillment of a contract created between the student and the institution.

column1: 6. Charging a Fee for Free Speech
column2: Directly or Indirectly

column1: SCENARIO: Your student group has invited a controversial speaker to campus. Suddenly
column2: your university informs you that your group is responsible for hundreds of dollars in additional “security fees” because the speaker’s lecture may anger protestors. Must your group pay these fees?

column1: FIRE continues to see numerous cases where colleges and universities have given the administration or campus police complete discretion to decide how much groups should pay for insurance
column2: security
column3: or other costs. Because these practices often include broad administrative discretion
column4: which could easily be used to silence any viewpoint
column5: they are usually unconstitutional. After all
column6: freedom of speech means little if administrators may effectively prevent certain views from being aired on campus simply by charging those students who wish to facilitate such discussion more than they can afford.

column1: For example
column3: the University of Colorado Boulder informed student groups involved in bringing Ward Churchill and William Ayers to campus that they would be billed over two thousand dollars for security costs on the basis of a perceived potential for a hostile audience reaction. After FIRE intervened
column4: the request was dropped. Similarly
column6: FIRE won victories for free expression and against such fees for student groups at the University of California Berkeley
column7: where students were charged thousands of dollars in security fees for bringing Elan Journo to campus for a speech on “America’s Stake in the Arab-Israeli Conflict
column8: ” and also at the University of Massachusetts Amherst
column9: where a student group was charged a $725 security fee for a speech by Don Feder regarding “hate crimes.”

column1: FIRE won these cases by pointing out to these public universities that when they seek to impose security fees on the basis of the perceived or predicted potential for a hostile audience reaction
column2: legal precedent is entirely against them. A Supreme Court case called Forsyth County v. Nationalist Movement (1992) dealt with a provision of a county ordinance declaring that the cost of protecting demonstrators on public property should be charged to the demonstrators themselves if that cost exceeded the usual cost of law enforcement. A county administrator was given the authority to assess the strain on public resources that various demonstrations would have and to adjust the security costs accordingly. In overturning this ordinance as unconstitutional
column3: the Supreme Court explained that any policy imposing charges on speech
column4: when those charges are based on an official’s estimation of the likely disruption
column5: necessarily requires an evaluation of the content of the message
column6: and
column7: therefore
column8: both could and likely would be used to censor speech. Under the policy declared unconstitutional in Forsyth
column9: your university would be free to prevent any group it did not like from holding an event
column10: simply by charging those groups prohibitively high rates. Censorship by roundabout means is as unconstitutional as direct and open censorship.

column1: Even if your university policy removes the discretion of school administrators and charges all students a flat rate for security and insurance
column2: you may still wish to challenge the policy on moral and educational grounds. You should point out to your administration that campuses should welcome free speech
column3: including protests and demonstrations
column4: as a valuable part of the educational environment. Furthermore
column5: students already pay
column6: through tuition and fees
column7: for the campus security they enjoy. Part of what you are paying for is the protection of your right to free speech
column8: including your right to hear the views of others. If there is any charge for expressive activities
column9: the charge should be borne by all students
column10: not by the individual groups—otherwise
column11: passive students will be rewarded for their lack of public activity while those contributing to the vitality of campus life will be taxed for being politically active.

column1: While it might be reasonable to levy security charges on large commercial events (like concerts or productions)
column2: where the events generate funds from which such costs logically could and should be paid
column3: FIRE sees no reason why students wishing to carry out peaceful demonstrations (and peaceful events are the only kind allowed under any university’s policies) should be taxed for their exercise of free expression.

column1: For more on the unconstitutional use of security fees on campus
column2: see former FIRE Justice Robert H. Jackson Legal Fellow Erica Goldberg’s article
column3: “Must Universities ‘Subsidize’ Controversial Ideas?: Allocating Security Fees When Student Groups Host Divisive Speakers
column4: ” George Mason University Civil Rights Law Journal
column5: Vol. 21
column6: No. 3

column1: 7. Newspaper Theft
SCENARIO: You are the editor of a college student paper
column2: and you decide to run a column that is critical of a campus student group. When your paper goes to print and is distributed throughout the campus
column3: the student group that you have criticized seizes virtually every copy of your publication and throws it out. Is there anything you can do?

column1: Newspaper thefts are far too common on university campuses and represent a vigilante form of censorship as dangerous to free expression as any act by the campus administration. The hardest part of the case may be proving that the papers were stolen and not legitimately picked up. Fortunately
column2: many of these would-be censors simply drop them in nearby dumpsters
column3: making proving foul play a great deal easier.

column1: If you believe that your paper has been stolen in order to suppress your point of view
column2: make certain that the entire campus
column3: including the administration
column4: knows about the theft. Some states and municipalities have passed or are considering legislation that would make newspaper thefts a crime even if the newspaper is distributed for free. For example
column5: the state of Maryland
column6: faced with a string of such thefts
column7: already has a law against them in its code
column8: and the city of Berkeley
column9: California
column10: passed such a law in 2003
column11: following the mass theft of a student newspaper. Indeed
column12: in most states
column13: such theft
column14: even if the newspaper is distributed for free
column15: might still constitute a crime
column16: such as malicious destruction of property or conspiracy to violate civil rights. Either way
column17: your school has a duty to protect your free speech rights from mob and vigilante rule. Call the administration out on this
column18: point out any double standard they might have applied for different publications
column19: and if they do not budge
column20: let FIRE and local and national media know. Universities may be indifferent to the book-burning mentality of some members of the campus community
column21: but the general public (including alumni and donors) are usually appalled by and react strongly against any university that allows the mob to silence minority or unpopular points of view. Also
column22: the nation’s newspapers and other media understand full well the nightmare and the danger to liberty of such destruction and suppression of the published word.

column1: 8. Investigating Protected Speech: University of Alaska Fairbanks

SCENARIO: You have authored a poem deploring the sexual abuse of young women among native Alaskans. Native Alaskan student activists protest and attempt to have you punished. The administration initiates an investigation. When you contact these administrators to tell them that they cannot punish you for exercising artistic expression
column2: they reply that their action is fine because
column3: so far
column4: it is “only an investigation.” What can you say in response?

column1: This situation happened to a professor of English at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. If your school tells you not to worry because it is only investigating you for your speech
column2: do not accept this explanation. If the university were to investigate speech every time someone reports offense
column3: the result would be the same as if it actually punished the speaker: people would avoid speaking
column4: especially on controversial topics
column5: in order to avoid being investigated.

column1: The president of the entire University of Alaska system
column2: after discussion with FIRE
column3: eventually intervened and put an end to such administrative dangers to the Constitution. He informed administrators at Fairbanks and at all Alaska campuses that in matters of controversial speech
column4: “There is nothing to investigate.” By taking a stand against scrutinizing clearly protected expression
column5: the president earned a reputation as a defender of free speech and was publicly celebrated for his act. His defense of the Constitution and of academic freedom was commended by Alaska’s Democratic governor
column6: by its Republican senators
column7: and by a bipartisan resolution of the state legislature. His example should serve as a model to university presidents who are tempted to bow to the pressure of would-be censors.

column1: 9. Rough Times for Satire and Parody: Harvard Business School

SCENARIO: You are an editor of the primary student newspaper at a professional school of a private university. You publish a cartoon that mocks the Career Services office for a series of serious and debilitating computer blunders during the crucial week of students’ career interviews. After the cartoon runs
column2: you are summoned into a top administrator’s office
column3: scolded for the article
column4: told to print more friendly things about the school
column5: and informed that you will be held personally accountable for any future objectionable content. You are also told to consider this meeting a “verbal warning
column6: ” the first level of sanction at your school. Can they do this?

column1: This scenario took place at Harvard Business School (HBS). The HBS paper published an editorial cartoon that criticized the school’s Career Services for severe and chronic technical problems during “Hell Week” (the time when HBS students go through the job interview process). The cartoon showed a computer screen with pop-up announcements about the problems with
column2: and inefficiency of
column3: Career Services. One announcement had two words expressing the exasperation of HBS students: “incompetent morons.”

column1: FIRE became involved after the Dean of HBS publicly defended the school’s behavior toward the editor. In one email to all students at HBS
column2: the Dean wrote: “Regardless of the role(s) we play on campus
column3: each of us first and foremost is a member of the Harvard Business School community
column4: and as such
column5: we are expected to treat each other respectfully. Referring to members of our community as ‘incompetent morons’ does not fall within the realm of respectful discourse.” While the Dean enjoys his own right to free expression and may criticize the editor
column6: this comment indicated a willingness to punish “disrespectful” speech and suggested that failing to meet the school’s “expectations” of civility would result in discipline. This case represents a classic example of an administration’s appeal to civility and respect as a pretext for allowing the administration to exercise far-reaching powers. Be very careful any time a dean uses “the community” as an excuse for punishing speech. You are part of the community; do not let the administration argue that it must censor speech to please the community. The idea that there is a conflict between free speech and the academic community fundamentally misunderstands both the goals of higher education and the nature and role of free speech.

column1: As FIRE stated in its letter to HBS:
It is generally taken for granted by deans of major universities that they
column2: their staff
column3: and their programs will be criticized
column4: lampooned
column5: and satirized. Deans usually handle this natural part of their job with grace and understanding. Threatening a student for publishing an editorial cartoon unbecomes a great liberal arts institution. Is the administration of HBS too weak to live with freedom? Are HBS students unworthy of the protections that any community college would have to offer under the Bill of Rights?

column1: Because Harvard is a private university
column2: our letter also noted:

column1: While you claim to encourage “debate
column2: discussion
column3: and dialogue
column4: ” the parameters you establish for allowable speech are as narrow as those of the most oppressive censors. A rule that outlaws speech that offends administrative power is not compatible with—and teaches contempt for—the most basic components of freedom. If you have such a rule
column5: FIRE expects that you will immediately notify all students
column6: prospective students
column7: and faculty members at Harvard Business School of the changes in policy and the end of freedom of speech at your institution. To advertise the critical and intellectual freedom of Harvard University and then to deliver repression of freedom is a “bait-and-switch” that HBS should know to be unethical
column8: if not a material breach of contract.

column1: After FIRE’s letter and the national attention that surrounded this case
column2: HBS reversed course. In a letter to FIRE
column3: the administration apologized and affirmed its commitment to free speech at HBS. If only all universities were so willing to acknowledge and correct their mistakes.

column1: 10. Allegedly Threatening or Intimidating Speech: San Diego State University

SCENARIO: You overhear several students loudly celebrating the success of a recent terrorist attack that claimed thousands of American lives. You approach the students and chide them emotionally and morally for their opinions
column2: which are offensive to you
column3: but you never threaten them. The students
column4: who outnumber you four to one
column5: charge you with “abusive behavior” for confronting them about their speech.

column1: This situation took place shortly after the attacks of September 11
column3: at San Diego State University (SDSU) and involved a student named Zewdalem Kebede. In response to the university’s investigation of Kebede
column4: FIRE wrote:

column1: Zewdalem Kebede’s right to speak applies even if his language was found to be emotional or fervent. The United States Supreme Court decided long ago
column2: in Cohen v. California (1971)
column3: that the expressive and emotive element of speech enjoys the full protection of the First Amendment. FIRE noted with irony that a university purporting to value diversity appears unable to tolerate diverse modes of discussion and debate
column4: which differ profoundly from nation to nation or individual to individual. By this action
column5: San Diego State University endangers speech on any topic that incites students’ feelings and emotions
column6: leaving only the most sterile and innocuous topics safe for analysis and debate.

column1: While the school is completely within its rights to punish “true threats” (for example
column2: “I am going to kill you
column3: Jim” becomes a true threat if it is a serious expression of an intent to commit violence that leaves Jim in fear of bodily harm or death)
column4: it must remember that the emotion attached to speech is part of the reason why it is valuable and needs protection.

column1: After receiving FIRE’s letter and attracting considerable negative media attention
column2: SDSU decided not to punish Mr. Kebede. Most colleges and universities routinely call upon students to “confront” racist or sexist speech whenever and wherever they overhear it. It is highly likely that SDSU was far from viewpoint neutral in its original investigation of Kebede.

column1: 11. Restrictions on Religious Speech or Association: University of North Carolina
SCENARIO: You are member of a Christian association that allows any student to join. The rules of your organization
column2: however
column3: require that in order to serve in the leadership of the organization
column4: you must be a practicing Christian. You get a letter from the school saying that your organization will lose recognition (be derecognized) because its rule constitutes “religious discrimination.” Could this be right?

column1: This remarkable situation has happened on a troubling number of campuses throughout the country. Typically in these cases
column2: a university maintains regulations that prohibit student organizations from discriminating against individuals on the basis of religion
column3: sexual orientation
column4: and other grounds. Therefore
column5: the university argues
column6: groups that “discriminate” by requiring their leadership to share their core beliefs
column7: even if these groups are religious or sectarian in nature
column8: must lose campus recognition
column9: which typically means that the group cannot hold meetings on campus
column10: has a limited ability to advertise its existence
column11: and is denied funding from student fees.

column1: FIRE believes that university regulations on antidiscrimination cannot trump the protections of the First Amendment. The First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause combined with First Amendment protections for free speech and free association—not to mention decency and common sense—should permit religious organizations to use their religious principles to select their leaders. (For more information on this topic
column2: please consult FIRE’s Guide to Religious Liberty on Campus. ) However
column3: recent legal developments have changed the jurisprudential landscape on this question.

column1: In the Supreme Court case Christian Legal Society v. Martinez (2010)
column2: the Supreme Court held that Hastings College of the Law did not violate the First Amendment rights of the student group Christian Legal Society by denying it official recognition under the school’s “all comers” policy
column3: which required all recognized student groups to accept any student who wished to join. Hastings’ “all comers” policy mandated that student groups accept even those students who do not agree with the group’s core beliefs
column4: including into leadership positions. The Court found that Hastings’ “all comers” policy was viewpoint-neutral and reasonable in light of the purposes served by the student organization forum. As such
column5: the Court held that the school’s decision to deny recognition to CLS
column6: due to the group’s requirement that voting members and officers sign a “Statement of Faith” indicating agreement with the group’s beliefs
column7: did not violate the student group’s freedom of association under the First Amendment.

column1: FIRE does not agree with the Court’s 5-4 decision for several reasons
column2: but particularly because the Court ignores CLS’ right to freedom of expressive association—that is
column3: the right to join together with others of like mind to promote a common message
column4: a right recognized by the Court in other cases and contexts. This right is guaranteed to student groups on public university campuses. For example
column5: students who are dedicated to a particular cause can band together
column6: combine resources
column7: hold meetings
column8: craft their shared vision
column9: and thus more effectively reach their fellow students with their message. The freedom of expressive association also includes the freedom not to associate—that is
column10: a group has the right to exclude those who do not share the group’s beliefs. Otherwise
column11: a group might lose control of the message it wants to articulate. So
column12: by requiring student groups on public campuses to admit all students as voting members and leaders
column13: regardless of whether or not these students actually agree with a given group’s core beliefs
column14: Martinez infringes heavily upon the First Amendment right to freedom of expressive association.

column1: There are several relevant Supreme Court cases here. Rosenberger v. University of Virginia (1995) holds that any regulation that bans religious student groups from equal participation in student-fee funding discriminates on the basis of viewpoint and is unconstitutional. The Supreme Court followed Rosenberger with its decision in University of Wisconsin v. Southworth (2000)
column2: which required that student fees be distributed on a strictly viewpoint-neutral basis. It ruled that the beliefs of the organization cannot be taken into account when distributing student funds. The final link in this chain of cases on freedom of association and viewpoint neutrality is Boy Scouts of America v. Dale (2000)
column3: in which the Court states that a group’s right to associate freely
column4: another right protected by the First Amendment
column5: is destroyed if it is not allowed the freedom to choose its own leadership. Any one of these cases should make it clear that derecognizing a religious student group because it wishes to have religious leadership is a violation of that group’s rights of free speech
column6: freedom of association
column7: and free exercise of religion.

column1: It is important to remember
column2: however
column3: that despite the harm done to associational rights on campus
column4: Martinez does not affect the broad speech protections that individual students enjoy. The Court reaffirmed that
column5: although an “all comers” policy may be constitutional in its eyes
column6: college administrators are not permitted to craft policies that discriminate on the basis of viewpoint. Quoting from earlier precedent
column7: the Martinez Court noted that a public university may not restrict speech “simply because it finds the views expressed by [a] group to be abhorrent.” Further
column8: the Martinez ruling is a narrow one. The Court held that an “all comers” policy is constitutional
column9: but only if the policy is evenly applied and does not target certain groups on the basis of their viewpoints
column10: and only if it reflects “reasonable” educational goals. Martinez did not hold that an “all comers” policy is required
column11: desirable
column12: effective
column13: or even practical.

column1: Indeed
column2: enforcing an “all comers” policy in practice will likely be incredibly difficult. For one
column3: an “all comers” policy renders colleges powerless to stop members of rival or opposing student groups from joining
column4: spying on
column5: taking over
column6: or simply diluting the message espoused by other groups. For example
column7: under an “all comers” policy
column8: atheists cannot be prevented from joining Muslim groups
column9: voting themselves into leadership positions
column10: and then voting to disband or change the mission of the group. Members of the College Democrats would be unable to stop College Republicans (and vice versa) from listening in on strategy meetings or even casting critical votes on strategic decisions. Actions like these would obviously lead to increased bitterness and rancor among groups on campus
column11: yet they would be almost unavoidable under an “all comers” policy.

column1: Additionally
column2: an “all comers” policy would be nearly impossible to enforce fairly. Any college adopting such a policy must prevent La Raza from excluding students who are hostile to Mexican immigration and an environmentalist student group from denying voting membership to global-warming skeptics. Meanwhile
column3: conservative and liberal newspapers alike will be attacked by their critics
column4: who will bring into question whether such time-honored publications have a right to exist at all under an “all comers” policy. Unless a college is absolutely confident that it has addressed every such requirement in every recognized student group
column5: it risks legal liability for violating the CLS v. Martinez mandate that enforcement of an “all comers” policy be evenhanded.

column1: Perhaps most importantly
column2: an “all comers” policy ultimately subjects freedom of association to the limits of tolerance among campus majorities
column3: impairing the intellectual and cultural diversity among groups that is vital on college campuses. A liberal education progresses in great measure through learning from different groups with distinct identities and opinions as those groups express their unique messages on campus. Diluting those messages through an “all comers” policy contracts rather than expands the marketplace of ideas across campus.

column1: 12. Double Standards: University of California
column2: San Diego

column1: SCENARIO: You are an editor at a humor and satire magazine at a public university
column2: and your publication often causes controversy. The administration has publicly condemned your paper multiple times and tried through a variety of ways to shut it down. Now
column3: your paper is charged with a minor infraction
column4: but it appears that the paper will lose funding from student fees and be disbanded if you are found guilty. It is clear that the administration is targeting your controversial content by punishing your paper so harshly. What should you do?

column1: This situation happened to The Koala
column2: a student publication that satirizes and parodies everything and everyone at the University of California
column3: San Diego (UCSD). University representatives had harshly condemned the publication on numerous occasions
column4: including once stating: “On behalf of the UCSD community
column5: we condemn The Koala’s abuse of the Constitutional guarantees of free expression and disfavor their unconscionable behavior.” (The only “behavior” engaged in was constitutionally protected expression.) UCSD’s administration is entitled to its own opinions
column6: but it then proceeded to lodge a series of dubious charges against the paper for numerous alleged infractions
column7: charges that reflected a patently obvious double standard.

column1: While preparing to help The Koala
column2: FIRE uncovered the fact that the very same vice chancellor who now condemned The Koala had issued—at another time—a ringing endorsement of the freedom of expression of another campus paper. In 1995
column3: the radical Hispanic student paper Voz Fronteriza ran an editorial that urged the murder of Hispanic agents of the Immigration and Naturalization Service and celebrated the fact that one had died while doing his job. “All Migra pigs should be killed
column4: every single one. … It is time to organize an anti-Migra patrol
column5: ” Voz Fronteriza wrote in its May 1995 issue. In response to calls for censorship and punishment issued by an outraged public and by members of Congress
column6: the vice chancellor stated: “The University is legally prohibited from censuring the content of student publications. … Previous attempts by universities and other entities to regulate freedom of speech
column7: including hate speech
column8: have all been ruled unconstitutional.” He also wrote that Voz Fronteriza had “the right to publish their views without adverse administrative action.” While
column9: in FIRE’s view
column10: Voz Fronteriza did have the right to publish that editorial
column11: it is far closer to the line of unprotected speech (see the earlier sidebar on incitement) than anything that ever came from The Koala .

column1: FIRE confronted UCSD with this breathtaking double standard
column2: shortly after which The Koala was found innocent of the charges against it. The lesson of this case is that many college administrators can be both grossly unfair and wildly inconsistent. They fervently protect speech with which they agree or sympathize
column3: while punishing the speech of the students whose views they do not like. It may be wise and particularly useful to look into the history of the administrators who are trying to censor you. You may well find that in previous instances they have supported (or not opposed) free speech in situations involving different points of view. Armed with this information
column4: you should demand that the administration live up to the positions taken in other cases. Double standards and hypocrisy are the enemies of liberty and honesty
column5: and they shame their practitioners when revealed.

column1: 13. Controversial Websites on University Servers
SCENARIO: Your university allows any enrolled student to have a website on the university server. You
column2: along with hundreds of other students
column3: maintain a website that includes information about yourself
column4: as well as information on topics that you think others might find interesting. One web page includes your thoughts about a company that you believe is actually a harmful pyramid scheme. The company contacts the web administrator
column5: claiming that he will sue the university unless it shuts down the “libelous” website. The school not only complies
column6: immediately shutting down your website
column7: but also brings you up on disciplinary charges
column8: including the charge that you failed to use your website solely for “study-related work.” What can you do?

column1: A situation very similar to this happened to a student at a public university in California. FIRE wrote to the school and explained that: 1) the student’s speech represented true political speech
column2: the kind of speech the First Amendment most clearly protects; 2) the university had created something similar to a limited public forum (see above) by granting all students web privileges and
column3: therefore
column4: could not discriminate against the student on the basis of his viewpoint; 3) the university instantly and unfairly assumed that the website was illegal and immediately turned on its own student; 4) the university’s claim that websites had to be related to academic work did not describe the actual practice at the university; 5) singling out only one website because of dubious complaints was inconsistent with its own rules and practice
column5: and demonstrated an intolerable double standard; and 6) the university would most likely be immune from a lawsuit for the content that its students post to their own web pages
column6: even if those pages are on the university server
column7: if it explicitly refrained from editorial control over those websites. In the light of all these considerations
column8: the school had no reason (and no excuse) to shut down the student’s website.

column1: The university eventually compromised. It should be noted
column2: however
column3: that the law regarding websites hosted on university servers is unclear and in a state of flux. While FIRE believes the arguments that it made to the university were legally sound
column4: there is no reasonable assurance that a court will interpret the university’s obligations in the same way. FIRE will closely monitor developments regarding the legal rights of students (and others) relating to website content on public servers and
column5: as always
column6: will argue forcefully for free speech and expression.

column1: 14. Obscenity: University of Memphis

SCENARIO: You participate in an Internet chat room composed of university students who openly and graphically discuss sexual topics and fantasies. When someone who posts to the site asks everyone what they find arousing
column2: you respond in explicit detail. Shortly thereafter
column3: you receive notification that your Internet access has been revoked and you face disciplinary charges for disseminating an “obscene” message. Is this really obscenity?

column1: While obscenity is a category of unprotected speech
column2: its legal definition actually covers only a quite narrow range of expression. As discussed in the earlier section on obscenity and the Miller test
column3: the Supreme Court has outlined three questions that must be asked and answered to determine if particular material is obscene: Whether the average person
column4: applying contemporary community standards
column5: would find that the work
column6: taken as a whole
column7: appeals to the “prurient interest” (an inordinate interest in sex) Whether the work depicts or describes
column8: in a patently offensive way
column9: sexual conduct Whether the work
column10: taken as a whole
column11: lacks serious literary
column12: artistic
column13: political
column14: or scientific value

column1: However
column2: online expression arguably has no geographic borders
column3: insofar as it is accessible by audiences across the nation (and indeed
column4: the world) and not just those physically nearby. The unprecedented interconnectivity of the internet has rendered Miller ’s “community standards” test more difficult to apply
column5: and courts have struggled to determine the utility of Miller with regard to online material. Some courts have concluded that a national community standard must be enforced
column6: lest the community most hostile to particular speech be effectively granted a veto over what the rest of the country might see. Other courts have continued to apply Miller ’s local community standard to online speech.

column1: But even given this evolving jurisprudence
column2: even things that would otherwise be considered obscenity in terms of graphic sexuality can be punished only if “the work
column3: taken as a whole
column4: lacks serious literary
column5: artistic
column6: political
column7: or scientific value.” If your vulgarity is for the sake of science
column8: art
column9: or politics
column10: it is not obscenity.

column1: A private school could choose to define its rules against “obscenity” as being less demanding than the Miller test. However
column2: if they use the word “obscenity” to describe banned expression but then seek to redefine it to cover a wider array of expression than the legal definition
column3: they run a risk of running afoul of the law and of your right to rely on the school’s written policies. As discussed above
column4: courts normally will interpret the university’s promises to its students in the way that the students are most likely to understand them.

column1: In the course of dealing with this case
column2: administrators at the University of Memphis were deluged by learned and compelling communications
column3: from across the country
column4: by defenders of civil liberties and the First Amendment. After months of such lessons in the law
column5: the dean in charge of the case dropped all charges
column6: writing to the defendant that “the posting
column7: taken as a whole within the context of the ongoing political discussion on the newsgroup
column8: did not meet the three-part test for obscenity articulated by the United States Supreme Court in the Miller v. California case .” She concluded: “As an institution of higher education
column9: we are committed to … free speech and academic freedom
column10: and we recognize our role as a marketplace of ideas.” The moral? Never become fatalistic: College administrators
column11: often sincerely misinformed
column12: can be educated about rights and liberty.

column1: 15. Heckler’s Veto: Washington State University
SCENARIO: You stage a satirical musical on campus. Many find it offensive
column2: and some in attendance repeatedly disrupt the performance. Your university does nothing to stop the disruptive activity. Should it have done so?

column1: This scenario occurred at Washington State University
column2: where student playwright Chris Lee’s satirical performance of his Passion of the Musical so angered students that roughly forty students in attendance at the show’s final performance repeatedly stood up
column3: shouted threats of violence at the performers
column4: and disrupted the event. At one point
column5: the heckling was so severe that although Lee asked campus security to remove the hecklers
column6: they refused
column7: and instead asked Lee to change the lyrics to one of his songs in order “to avoid a possible riot or physical harm.”

column1: Amazingly
column2: FIRE discovered that Washington State’s Office for Campus Involvement had actually purchased the heckling students’ tickets to the performance. Lee’s later complaints to the university about the hecklers were dismissed; administrators claimed that because the play provoked and “taunted” the audience
column3: it exhibited “qualities of a public forum.” Even more amazingly
column4: the university’s president defended the hecklers’ actions
column5: telling a student newspaper that the hecklers had “exercised their rights of free speech in a very responsible manner by letting the writer and players know exactly how they felt.”

column1: Finally
column2: following intervention by FIRE and negative national media attention
column3: the university allowed Lee’s next controversial play to proceed without disruption. University administrators posted and read a note before each performance announcing that no disruptions would be tolerated and that hecklers would be escorted from the venue.

column1: The principles at stake here are of vital importance and should be clearly understood by all students
column2: faculty
column3: and administrators. When a university punishes someone because of the hostile reactions of others to his or her protected political speech
column4: they are conferring what is called a “heckler’s veto” upon anyone who would want to silence speech. The practical implications of conferring a heckler’s veto are devastating for a free society
column5: but especially for a university. If a university punishes people on the basis of how harshly or violently other people might react to their words
column6: it creates an incentive for those who disagree to react violently. This policy would confer veto power over speech upon the least tolerant and most dangerous members of society—an invitation to mob rule. It is extremely dangerous to all of our freedoms ever to grant a heckler’s veto.

column1: The free speech provisions of the First Amendment
column2: in practice
column3: exist primarily to protect unpopular speech. There would be little need for an amendment to protect only popular
column4: mainstream speech
column5: since the democratic process would protect that speech through its own mechanism of majority control. Universities have a positive duty to protect students and faculty from violence for stating their opinions. A college that would expel someone because of the violent reaction of others to his or her speech has its obligations completely backwards. It is the university’s duty to protect the speakers and to punish those who break the law by threatening them.

column1: 16. Controversial Speakers: Ithaca College
SCENARIO: You invite a controversial speaker to campus. When the speaker arrives
column2: several students attempt to have you arrested by campus police on charges of committing a “bias-related incident” (that is
column3: hate speech). Can they do this?

column1: This situation happened to the College Republicans at Ithaca College when they invited a speaker to campus to discuss “The Failures of Feminism.” Fortunately
column2: Ithaca declined to press charges
column3: but the case still represents the bizarre and extreme expectations created by campus harassment policies. The theory was that the speaker (female
column4: by the way) was so radical in her viewpoints that her speech constituted harassment of the entire community based on sex. This was
column5: of course
column6: just another attempt to silence unpopular speech on campus
column7: and though it would never pass constitutional muster if attempted at a public school
column8: students will likely try this approach again. If they do
column9: they should be reminded that such a broad definition of harassment is flatly unconstitutional. If this takes place at a private university
column10: however
column11: it is best to remind the administration that such a policy could be used to prevent any speaker from coming to campus
column12: and would guarantee ferocious battles over who should and should not be invited in the future
column13: and
column14: since every controversial speaker offends someone
column15: would lead either to silence or to double standards.

column1: As for the students who would try to use harassment polices in this way
column2: they should know that their example will become a cause célèbre and will be used by those who oppose all “bias-related harassment rules.” By trying in this way to censor their fellow students
column3: they bring disrepute not only to themselves
column4: but also to the very notion of protection from genuine harassment. Also
column5: of course
column6: they sacrifice the very grounds on which it would be possible to defend their own free speech rights against those whom they offend.

column1: 17. Unequal Access for Student Groups—Denying the Right to Freedom of Association: University of Miami
SCENARIO: You wish to start up a student group that discusses conservative philosophy
column2: and you apply for funding from student fees
column3: just like dozens of other groups at your public university. The student government
column4: which recognizes student groups
column5: refuses to recognize your group because
column6: it argues
column7: there is already one other recognized conservative group on campus
column8: namely
column9: the College Republicans. On the other hand
column10: the student government has formally recognized dozens of other closely related student groups. Can it deny funding to your group?

column1: This scenario happened at the University of Miami (UM). A group of women attempted to form a conservative organization
column2: Advocates for Conservative Thought (ACT). Its purpose was “the exposition and promotion of conservative principles and ideas.” ACT was repeatedly denied funding by UM
column3: because
column4: the student government claimed
column5: its intended purpose would “overlap” with the College Republicans and with one group that promoted nonpartisan political debate. FIRE wrote a letter to UM’s president
column6: pointing out that the school could not deny funding to one group because of its viewpoint while allowing dozens of other groups on the other side of the spectrum their individual recognition.

column1: Such discrimination against a group based purely on the proposed purpose and ideology of the group is in direct violation of the Supreme Court’s prohibitions against content-based and viewpoint discrimination. It also violates the same free association rights that applied in the scenario relating to freedom of religious association (see Scenario 11
column2: above).

column1: The Supreme Court has also established that each such freely organized group has the right to equal student funding at public universities
column2: and may not be discriminated against on the basis of the content of the group’s ideology. In University of Wisconsin v. Southworth (2000)
column3: the Court held that a public university must distribute funds equally to each recognized group on campus without any consideration of the organization’s viewpoint. Under Southworth
column4: if the university does not comply with this limitation
column5: it may not charge mandatory student fees to support extracurricular activities.

column1: No matter what your group’s ideology
column2: the purpose and content of your organization may not be grounds for denying your group official recognition as a student group. Furthermore
column3: there is a strong constitutional right of voluntary association that allows individuals to form groups with a purpose and content of their choosing. Your group may be denied recognition on other legitimate grounds (such as insufficient membership)
column4: but the purpose and belief system of your group should never be the factor that prevents your group from gaining recognition and equal access to the school’s resources.

column1: UM is a private university
column2: and not bound by Southworth
column3: but FIRE raised the issue of whether it was willing to deny its students the fundamental rights and legal equalities granted by any public college. In response to FIRE’s letter and press release
column4: the university president convened an urgent meeting. Immediately after the meeting
column5: ACT was informed that it would receive official recognition regardless of its content or purpose. UM President Donna Shalala wrote to FIRE to thank it for bringing this vital matter to her attention. The moral? Constitutional principles are so often not merely legal principles
column6: but moral principles
column7: as well. Colleges and universities ignore them to their shame and peril.

column1: 18. Political Activity on Campus: University of Oklahoma
SCENARIO: Prior to national elections
column2: your university sends out a campus-wide email announcing that students are forbidden from using university email accounts to “endorse or oppose a candidate
column3: including the forwarding of political humor/commentary.” Can the university institute such a broad ban?

column1: This precise scenario occurred at the University of Oklahoma
column2: which informed students and faculty via email a few months before the 2008 election that “[a]s a state agency … the University may not endorse or oppose a particular candidate for office
column3: ” and that this prohibition “includes the use by its faculty
column4: staff and students of its email and network systems.” The announcement further stipulated that the university’s email and network systems could not be used to send messages endorsing or opposing a candidate
column5: or even for forwarding “political humor/commentary.” The university’s (erroneous) rationale was that such discussion placed the school at risk of losing its tax exemption.

column1: This is a classic example of an overbroad ban on core political speech protected by the First Amendment. As FIRE reminded the university in a letter
column2: the school was banning speech protected by the First Amendment. Indeed
column3: we pointed out that the First Amendment was arguably designed to protect precisely this kind of political speech. Moreover
column4: the university’s rationale for silencing such a significant swath of student speech was flawed. The Internal Revenue Service has made clear that
column5: in the campus context
column6: the restriction on political activity placed on non-profit
column7: tax-exempt entities is interpreted differently in light of the educational mission of colleges and universities
column8: allowing certain activities (such as a political science class that requires students to work on a campaign
column9: as long as the student
column10: not the instructor
column11: is allowed to choose the campaign
column12: or political editorials in favor of candidates in a student newspaper) that would otherwise likely constitute prohibited activity for tax-exempt entities. Restrictions on political activity apply to the institution itself and those reasonably perceived to be speaking on its behalf
column13: not to individual students
column14: faculty
column15: or staff engaged in clearly individual
column16: unaffiliated activity.

column1: When contacted by FIRE
column2: the University of Oklahoma recognized the error of its ban on political speech. In a follow-up email
column3: a university official stated
column4: “The policy has been clarified to those who have raised questions. I felt that in addition it should be clarified to the entire university community.
