column1: 20. Bullying and “Cyberbullying”: When Can a University Punish a Student?
SCENARIO: In an isolated email
column2: you insult another student for his actions towards you. The student files a complaint against you
column3: alleging that you have “cyberbullied” him in contravention of the anti-bullying policy in the college’s Student Code of Conduct. May your college punish you?

column1: While FIRE has yet to see a case involving this precise set of facts
column2: it is sadly all too likely that one will be forthcoming soon. That is because federal and state legislators and education officials are increasingly pushing for new laws requiring schools
column3: including colleges and universities
column4: to institute sweeping policies aimed at prohibiting students from engaging in “bullying” and “cyberbullying.” These legislative pushes gained significant public support following the tragic suicide of a Rutgers college student in the fall of 2010. (The student had been subjected to a reprehensible invasion of privacy
column5: as his roommate allegedly posted online a video of him engaging in a sexual encounter with another male.) But—however tragic the circumstances that inspired it—the proposed legislation typically requires colleges to enact overbroad and vague bans on protected speech.

column1: For example
column2: in January 2011
column3: New Jersey passed legislation requiring every college to prohibit “harassment
column4: intimidation and bullying
column5: ” which it defined as:

column1: [A] single incident or a series of incidents
column2: that is reasonably perceived as being motivated either by any actual or perceived characteristic
column3: such as race
column4: color
column5: religion
column6: ancestry
column7: national origin
column8: gender
column9: sexual orientation
column10: gender identity and expression
column11: or a mental
column12: physical or sensory disability
column13: or by any other distinguishing characteristic
column14: that takes place on the property of the institution of higher education or at any function sponsored by the institution of higher education
column15: that substantially disrupts or interferes with the orderly operation of the institution or the rights of other students and that:

column1: (a) a reasonable person should know
column2: under the circumstances
column3: will have the effect of physically or emotionally harming a student or damaging the student’s property
column4: or placing a student in reasonable fear of physical or emotional harm to his person or damage to his property;

column1: (b) has the effect of insulting or demeaning any student or group of students; or
(c) creates a hostile educational environment for the student
(d) by interfering with a student’s education or by severely or pervasively causing physical or emotional harm to the student.
As you now know from what you have learned in this Guide
column2: such a sweeping prohibition is startlingly vague and broad. By censoring all student speech that “is reasonably perceived as being motivated either by any actual or perceived characteristic” and that “a reasonable person should know” will “have the effect of … emotionally harming a student” or “placing a student in reasonable fear of … emotional harm
column3: ” the state of New Jersey effectively requires all students on campus to step on proverbial eggshells every time they open their mouths. How is a “reasonable” student supposed to know whether his or her speech will place another student in “reasonable fear” of “emotional harm”—and what precisely is “emotional harm
column4: ” anyway? Because the answers to these questions are highly subjective
column5: New Jersey has left its students to guess at what speech is and is not prohibited on campus. The resulting chilling effect that is certain to follow raises very serious First Amendment concerns.

column1: Worse still
column2: New Jersey’s legislation ignores the fact that both “harassment” and “intimidation” are legal terms of art
column3: as discussed earlier in this Guide
column4: each with precise legal definitions fashioned by the Supreme Court in a way that appropriately balances the right to freedom of expression with the legitimate state interest in eliminating harassment and intimidation. As for “bullying
column5: ” it is impossible to see how conduct already prohibited by the Davis definition of harassment—that is
column6: behavior “so severe
column7: pervasive
column8: and objectively offensive that it effectively bars the victim’s access to an educational opportunity or benefit”—does not effectively cover the conduct usually labeled as “bullying.”

column1: Finally
column2: by forbidding speech that “has the effect of insulting or demeaning any student or group of students” in such a way as to “substantially disrupt[] or interfere[] with the orderly operation of the institution
column3: ” New Jersey has sanctioned the “heckler’s veto.” Imagine this scenario: The College Democrats harshly criticize the College Republicans’ position on an issue—that is
column4: the Democrats engage in speech motivated by the College Republicans’ “distinguishing characteristic” of being Republican. In response
column5: the Republicans substantially disrupt the college’s operation in some way—perhaps by covering the campus with graffiti. Under New Jersey law
column6: the Democrats may now be guilty of “harassment
column7: intimidation
column8: or bullying.” So
column9: in effect
column10: New Jersey has actually incentivized overreaction to any perceived insult
column11: since the “victim’s” disruption of the orderly operation of the school automatically shifts the blame to the speaker
column12: not to the student or students actually disrupting the school.

column1: All public colleges in New Jersey are now required to maintain and enforce this new kind of speech code. Unfortunately
column2: New Jersey may not be the only state requiring its colleges to enact similar restrictions on protected speech; indeed
column3: at the time of this writing
column4: a federal anti-bullying bill has been introduced in both chambers of Congress. In response to legislation like that described here
column5: or scenarios like the one presented above
column6: FIRE urges students to remember their rights. No state or federal legislation trumps your First Amendment right to freedom of expression or the rights guaranteed by state constitutions
column7: and you should argue forcefully for the principles of freedom of expression—not just to your fellow students
column8: though they surely are important
column9: but also to your deans
column10: faculty
column11: and the larger public. Remind them that in order to be a true marketplace of ideas
column12: our colleges and universities must honor the robust free expression rights that students require as a precondition of obtaining a modern liberal education. Let them know that harassment and intimidation are already excepted from First Amendment protection
column13: that much of the behavior we generally think of as “bullying” is already prohibited under state and federal anti-harassment law

SCENARIO: As a member of student government

column3: administrators
column4: and your fellow students. Your committee is concerned by a proposal to shorten the school year. To raise awareness of the planned changes amongst faculty members
column5: your committee approves you to send out an email to faculty detailing your concerns with the proposal. After sending your email to 400 faculty members out of the more than 5
column6: 000 at your large university

column1: First

column6: or political statements or purposes.”

column1: Second
column2: the policy’s application in this instance is egregiously wrongheaded. Spencer is a student government leader. Her speech was in conjunction with a formal student-faculty committee’s response to a significant change in the university calendar—a policy shift that

column1: Unfortunately for students at MSU and other schools that maintain similarly restrictive policies on email usage

column3: under the terms of MSU’s policy

column6: MSU’s insistence on keeping “personal opinions” out of campus email betrays a transparent desire to render all users guilty of violating university policy
column7: so as to enable selective prosecution at will on the basis of content. This is to say that because MSU surely recognizes that virtually all users of MSU email accounts will at some point use their account to “express personal opinions
column8: ” MSU’s stubborn demand that they refrain from doing so means that the policy will be broken by virtually everyone. As a result
column9: then

column1: 22. Fraternities
column2: Sororities
column3: and Freedom of Expression

column1: SCENARIO: Your fraternity or sorority is faced with possible dissolution. What associational rights does a fraternity or sorority have at a public university?
Generally speaking
column2: fraternities and sororities at public universities enjoy a right to freedom of association under the First Amendment
column3: which provides a degree of protection against administrative attempts to disband or dissolve Greek organizations. However
column4: fraternities and sororities should understand that courts have recognized three different types of freedom of association
column5: each of varying strength
column6: and that their collective activities as a group will impact the amount of First Amendment freedom of association protection they can expect to receive.

column1: The first—and strongest—form of freedom of association is intimate association
column2: best understood as familial in nature and most protected from governmental interference. As the Supreme Court noted in Roberts v. United States Jaycees (1984)
column3: “the constitutional shelter afforded such relationships reflects the realization that individuals draw much of their emotional enrichment from close ties with others.” The second form is the right to expressive association
column4: exemplified by groups organized around a shared set of beliefs—like religious groups
column5: volunteer societies
column6: political organizations
column7: and so forth. Courts have recognized that the First Amendment protects citizens who wish to join voices with those of like mind to amplify and espouse a common belief or message
column8: so the right to expressive association has been afforded significant protection. Again
column9: in Jaycees
column10: the Court observed that “[a]ccording protection to collective effort on behalf of shared goals is especially important in preserving political and cultural diversity and in shielding dissident expression from suppression by the majority.” The third and weakest form of freedom of association is social association
column11: which generally refers to groups of people brought together in common social activities
column12: but which lack a unifying commitment to advocacy of a message or belief and are more or less unselective and open to the public. The government has considerable power to regulate the activities of social associations.

column1: In determining which form of association a group may exemplify
column2: courts have looked to several determining characteristics
column3: identified by the Jaycees Court as including “size
column4: purpose
column5: policies
column6: selectivity
column7: congeniality
column8: and other characteristics that in a particular case may be pertinent.”

column1: While the legal precedent is not uniformly settled
column2: recent cases suggest that typical fraternities and sororities are most often engaged in social association. For example
column4: the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit found that the College of Staten Island’s decision to deny recognition to a fraternity that refused to comply with the university’s anti-discrimination policy (regarding the exclusion of women) did not present a violation of the group’s right to freedom of association. The Second Circuit
column5: after reviewing the fraternity’s size
column6: selectivity
column7: purpose
column8: and exclusion of non-members
column9: found that the group regularly opened events and parties to the public; advocated only for “broad
column10: public-minded goals that do not depend for their promotion on close-knit bonds”; and was relatively unselective in recruiting new members
column11: which it “recruit[ed] more widely and aggressively.” As a result of this general openness and lack of specific purpose or advocacy
column12: the court found the group’s associational rights were “relatively weak” and did not outweigh the government’s interest in enforcing its non-discrimination policy
column13: which the court further determined imposed “no great burden” on the group’s activities.

column1: Similarly
column3: the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit rejected a fraternity’s claim to expressive association rights by noting the fraternity’s failure to engage in expression:

column1: While the international organization of Pi Lambda Phi has an admirable history that includes being the country’s first non-sectarian fraternity
column2: there is no substantial evidence in the record that the University chapter of Pi Lambda has done anything to actively pursue the ideals underlying this stance. Although members of the Chapter claimed in their deposition testimony that the Chapter still promotes these ideals
column3: they did not give any specific examples of how it does so. Furthermore
column4: while Pi Lambda Phi’s international organization runs various programs aimed at individual development
column5: there is no evidence in the record that even a single member of the University chapter participated in any of these programs.

column1: The Chapter also points to a couple of relatively minor acts of charity performed in 1996 as proof of its expressive aspects
column2: but these are underwhelming. The Chapter represents that it once helped run a Halloween haunted house for the Pittsburgh School for the Blind
column3: raised $350 through selling raffle tickets for a charity called the Genesis House
column4: and ran a “Breakfast with Santa” to raise money for Genesis House. The Chapter’s counsel admitted at oral argument that this was the extent of the Chapter’s charitable activities. A few minor charitable acts do not alone make a group’s association expressive
column5: and community service must have more than a merely incidental relationship to the group’s character for such service to implicate the constitutional protection of expressive association. The Chapter has not shown in the record that its sporadic acts of community service are related to its basic nature or goals.

column1: Given these opinions
column2: it seems clear that fraternities and sororities interested in making successful freedom of association claims must do more than simply throw parties and live in a common area together—activities which leave them classifiable as simply social associations
column3: and thus worthy of precious little First Amendment protection. If
column4: instead
column5: fraternities and sororities chose to take visible public stances in support of their ideals or a chosen group message or cause
column6: they would be more likely to qualify as an expressive association. In other words
column7: the more a fraternity or sorority is able to demonstrate that it engages in the advocacy of a shared message in a way that depends on group membership
column8: the stronger the group’s claim that it is properly considered an expressive association
column9: with all the attendant First Amendment protection. If
column10: having read this
column11: members of fraternities and sororities now seek a cause to publicly support
column12: FIRE suggests free speech on campus would be an excellent choice.

column1: Freud's way of interpretation has been called phallocentric by many contemporary thinkers. This is because
column2: for Freud
column3: the unconscious always desires the phallus (penis). Males are afraid of castration - losing their phallus or masculinity to another male. Females always desire to have a phallus - an unfulfillable desire. Thus boys resent their fathers (fear of castration) and girls desire theirs. For Freud
column4: desire is always defined in the negative term of lack - you always desire what you don't have or what you are not
column5: and it is very unlikely that you will fulfill this desire. Thus his psychoanalysis treatment is meant to teach the patient to cope with his or her insatiable desires.

column1: The life and death instincts
Freud believed that humans were driven by two conflicting central desires: the life drive ( Eros ) (incorporating the sex drive) and the death drive ( Thanatos ). Freud's description of Eros
column2: whose energy is known as libido
column3: included all creative
column4: life-producing drives. The death drive (or death instinct)
column5: whose energy is known as mortido
column6: represented an urge inherent in all living things to return to a state of calm: in other words
column7: an inorganic or dead state. He recognized Thanatos only in his later years and develops his theory on the death drive in Beyond the Pleasure Principle . Freud approaches the paradox between the life drives and the death drives by defining pleasure and unpleasure. According to Freud
column8: unpleasure refers to stimulus that the body receives. (For example
column9: excessive friction on the skin's surface produces a burning sensation; or
column10: the bombardment of visual stimuli amidst rush hour traffic produces anxiety.) Conversely
column11: pleasure is a result of a decrease in stimuli (for example
column12: a calm environment the body enters after having been subjected to a hectic environment). If pleasure increases as stimuli decreases
column13: then the ultimate experience of pleasure for Freud would be zero stimulus
column14: or death. Given this proposition
column15: Freud acknowledges the tendency for the unconscious to repeat unpleasurable experiences in order to desensitize
column16: or deaden
column17: the body. This compulsion to repeat unpleasurable experiences explains why traumatic nightmares occur in dreams
column18: as nightmares seem to contradict Freud's earlier conception of dreams purely as a site of pleasure
column19: fantasy
column20: and desire. On the one hand
column21: the life drives promote survival by avoiding extreme unpleasure and any threat to life. On the other hand
column22: the death drive functions simultaneously toward extreme pleasure
column23: which leads to death. Freud addresses the conceptual dualities of pleasure and unpleasure
column24: as well as sex/life and death
column25: in his discussions on masochism and sadomasochism . The tension between Eros and Thanatos represents a revolution in his manner of thinking. Some also refer to the death instinct as the Nirvana Principle.

column1: It should be added that these ideas owe a great deal to both Arthur Schopenhauer and Friedrich Nietzsche . Schopenhauer's pessimistic philosophy
column2: expounded in The World as Will and Representation
column3: describes a renunciation of the will to live that corresponds on many levels with Freud's Death Drive. The life drive clearly owes much to Nietzsche's concept of the Dionysian in The Birth of Tragedy . Freud was an avid reader of both philosophers and acknowledged their influence.

column1: Freud's legacy
Freud's theories and research methods were controversial during his life and still are so today
column2: but few dispute his huge impact on psychologists and the academically inclined.

column1: Most importantly
column2: Freud popularized the ""talking-cure""—an idea that a person could solve problems simply by talking over them
column3: something that was almost unheard of in the 19th century. Even though many psychotherapists today tend to reject the specifics of Freud's theories
column4: this basic mode of treatment comes largely from his work.

column1: Most of Freud's specific theories—like his stages of psychosexual development—and especially his methodology
column2: have fallen out of favor in modern experimental psychology .

column1: Some psychotherapists
column2: however
column3: still follow an approximately Freudian system of treatment. Many more have modified his approach
column4: or joined one of the schools that branched from his original theories (see Neo-Freudian ). Still others reject his theories entirely
column5: although their practice may still reflect his influence.

While he saw himself as a scientist

column3: a philosopher and main supporter of the ideas of the subconscious and empathy. [16] Freud's theories have had a tremendous impact on the humanities --especially on the Frankfurt school and critical theory . Freud's model of the mind is often criticized as an unsubstantiated challenge to the enlightenment model of rational agency
column4: which was a key element of much modern philosophy . Rationality While many enlightenment thinkers viewed rationality as both an unproblematic ideal and a defining feature of man
column5: Freud's model of the mind drastically reduced the scope and power of reason. In Freud's view
column6: reasoning occurs in the conscious mind--the ego--but this is only a small part of the whole. The mind also contains the hidden
column7: irrational elements of id and superego
column8: which lie outside of conscious control
column9: drive behavior
column10: and motivate conscious activities. As a result
column11: these structures call into question humans' ability to act purely on the basis of reason
column12: since lurking motives are also always at play. Moreover
column13: this model of the mind makes rationality itself suspect
column14: since it may be motivated by hidden urges or societal forces (e.g. defense mechanisms
column15: where reasoning becomes ""rationalizing""). Transparency of Self Freud challenged the idea of empiricists such as John Locke and David Hume that the workings of the mind can be understood by introspection. He considered many central aspects of a person remain radically inaccessible to the conscious mind (without the aid of psychotherapy).

column1: Critical reactions
Although Freud's theories were influential

column4: called Freud's dream theory ""dangerously inaccurate"" and noted that ""rank confabulations...appear to hold water
column5: psychoanalytically"" [17] . The philosopher A. C. Grayling has said that ""Philosophies that capture the imagination never wholly fade....But as to Freud's claims upon truth
column6: the judgment of time seems to be running against him."" [18] Peter D. Kramer
column7: a psychiatrist and faculty member of Brown Medical School
column8: said ""I'm afraid [Freud] doesn't hold up very well at all. It almost feels like a personal betrayal to say that. But every particular is wrong: the universality of the Oedipus complex
column9: penis envy
column10: infantile sexuality."" A 2006 article in Newsweek magazine called him ""history's most debunked doctor."" [19]

column1: Freud's theories are often criticized for not being real science. [20] This objection was raised by Karl Popper
column2: who claimed that all proper scientific theories must be potentially falsifiable . Popper argued that no experiment or observation could ever falsify Freud's theories of psychology (e.g. someone who denies having an Oedipal complex is interpreted as repressing it)
column3: and thus they could not be considered scientific. [21]
